E061 (Cook to Diffie-Hellman) is interpretive

CS029.problem: As programs grew to many thousands of lines, they had to be divided among programmers and into parts that could be written, understood and changed separately. The usual method was to split the program along the steps of its flowchart: read the input, process it, write the output. But the parts of such a design all depended on the same data formats, so one change, say to how data was stored, forced changes in every part. Dividing a system into modules was recognised as essential, but there was no good guidance on where to draw the lines.
CS029.insight: David Parnas compared two ways of building the same small program, a keyword-in-context index. The first followed the flowchart; the second divided the work according to design decisions likely to change, with each module hiding one such decision, such as how the text is stored or how lines are sorted. Other modules could use it only through a small, stable interface and had to know nothing about its internals. This principle, information hiding, gave a criterion for decomposing a system: not by what happens when, but by what is likely to change. Hidden decisions can then be changed, or work done in parallel, without disturbing the rest.
CS029.analogy: A wall socket is an interface that hides the power station. You do not care how the electricity is generated, and the utility can change how it does so without anyone replacing their appliances.
CS029.unlocked: Information hiding became a central principle of software design. It underlies abstract data types, encapsulation in object-oriented languages, module and package systems, and the idea of an API as a contract that lets teams work independently. It shaped how software architects think about change, and, decades later, the boundaries between services in large distributed systems. Parnas went on to develop methods for specifying module interfaces precisely and for software documentation.
CS029.left_open: The principle says to hide what is likely to change, but it cannot tell you what will change; guessing wrong leaves the structure fighting you. Hiding has costs, such as extra calls and layers that can slow a system down. The example is small, and the paper does not show how to specify an interface precisely enough that others can rely on it, or how to cope with modules whose changes are connected. Too much modularity can also fragment a system into pieces that are hard to follow.
CS029.diagram_alt: Two ways to split a program. On the left, modules follow the flowchart steps and all depend on one shared data format. On the right, each module hides one design decision, such as line storage or alphabetizing, behind a small interface.
review: The example in the paper is a KWIC (keyword in context) index

CS030.problem: Large databases and file systems keep their data on disks, where reading a block takes thousands of times longer than reading memory. To find a record quickly you need an index, an ordered structure that points to where the data is. The usual tree structures were designed for memory, one key per node, so finding a record in a million could mean twenty or more disk reads. They also became lopsided as records were added and removed, and rebalancing them was awkward. A disk-based index needed to be shallow, stay balanced, and be cheap to update.
CS030.insight: Rudolf Bayer and Edward McCreight, at Boeing, designed a tree whose nodes are as wide as a disk page, each holding hundreds of keys and pointers. Because a node has so many children, the tree is very shallow: a few levels can index millions of records, so a search reads only a handful of pages. The rule that keeps it balanced is simple: every leaf is at the same depth and every node is at least half full. Inserting into a full node splits it in two and pushes the middle key up to the parent; deleting from a node that gets too empty merges it with a neighbour. The tree balances itself, in guaranteed logarithmic time.
CS030.analogy: Picture a library’s card catalogue where each drawer’s dividers point to other drawers. A few steps take you to any card among a million, and when a drawer overflows, you split it in two and add a divider above.
CS030.unlocked: B-trees, and the B+ tree variant that keeps all data in the leaves, became the standard index structure. They sit inside nearly every relational database, from Oracle and DB2 to PostgreSQL and MySQL, and inside many file systems. They made the fast, interactive queries of relational systems possible. More broadly, the paper showed how to design data structures around the cost of the storage hierarchy, minimising transfers rather than counting steps, an idea that carries on in external-memory algorithms.
CS030.left_open: B-trees assume that reading a page is expensive and writing is similar to reading, which flash storage and large memories changed. Updating a B-tree in place can mean many small random writes, and for write-heavy workloads log-structured designs, such as the log-structured merge trees behind many modern stores, often do better. Allowing many users to read and update the tree at once needs careful locking that the original paper did not cover.
CS030.diagram_alt: A B-tree: a root holding two keys, 30 and 60, pointing to three child pages holding further keys, so a search takes only a few page reads. A note says that when a page overflows it is split and the middle key moves up.
review: Bayer and McCreight were at Boeing Scientific Research Laboratories
B+ trees keep all records in the leaves and are what most databases actually use

CS031.problem: Cook had shown that one problem, satisfiability, is as hard as any problem whose answers can be checked quickly. But the world was full of other stubborn problems: scheduling jobs, packing items, routing a salesperson through cities, colouring maps, finding groups of mutual friends. Operations researchers and mathematicians had tried for years to find fast exact methods for them, with no success and no explanation. It was not clear whether these problems were related to Cook’s, or whether his result was a curiosity about logic.
CS031.insight: Richard Karp showed that it is not a curiosity. He took Cook’s problem and, using polynomial-time reductions, converted it into other problems, and those into still more, building a web of twenty-one well-known combinatorial problems, including clique, vertex cover, the travelling salesman’s cycle (Hamiltonian circuit), set covering, knapsack and graph colouring. Each reduction shows that if the second problem could be solved quickly, so could the first. Since every problem in NP reduces to satisfiability, all twenty-one are NP-complete: as hard as each other and as hard as every problem in the class. It explained why so many separate efforts had failed: they were all attacking the same hard core in different disguises.
CS031.analogy: It is like discovering that twenty-one apparently unrelated puzzles are secretly the same puzzle in different costumes. Solve one quickly and you have solved them all; fail to solve any of them, and you now know why.
CS031.unlocked: Karp’s paper turned NP-completeness from a theorem into a toolkit. Within a few years thousands of problems from every field were shown to be NP-complete, collected in Garey and Johnson’s 1979 book. For practitioners, recognising a problem as NP-complete became the signal to move to heuristics, approximations or special cases instead of searching forever for an exact fast method. The reduction technique also underlies later work on approximation and on what cannot be computed efficiently. Karp received the Turing Award in 1985.
CS031.left_open: Reductions show that problems are equally hard relative to each other, not that they are hard: the question of whether P equals NP remains open, so the entire web could in principle collapse into easy problems. Worst-case hardness says little about the typical instance, which can be easy in practice. And the theory sorts problems coarsely: it does not say how well they can be approximated, or what happens for problems, such as factoring, that seem to lie between easy and NP-complete.
CS031.diagram_alt: A web of problems linked by arrows of reduction, starting from satisfiability and 3-satisfiability and reaching clique, vertex cover, Hamiltonian circuit, chromatic number, exact cover and knapsack. If any one is solved quickly, all can be.
review: Karp's paper dates from 1972 (proceedings of the 1972 symposium); the CSV lists 1973
The paper lists 21 problems; the diagram shows only a sample of the reductions
Karp received the 1985 Turing Award; Garey and Johnson's book appeared in 1979

CS032.problem: By the early 1970s several packet-switched networks existed, among them the ARPANET, a packet radio network and a satellite network. Each used its own packet sizes, addressing and rules for handling lost or reordered data, and none could talk to another. The ARPANET’s own protocol assumed the network itself would deliver everything reliably, which was not true of radio or satellite links. Researchers wanted a way to join different networks into one, without forcing them all to become the same.
CS032.insight: Vinton Cerf and Robert Kahn proposed a common protocol that runs in the computers at the edges of the networks, with gateways joining the networks in between. Data is sent as packets, called datagrams, carrying addresses of the form network and host, which gateways forward without needing to understand what is inside. The network is assumed to be unreliable, so reliability is built at the ends: the receiving program acknowledges what it gets, numbered packets are reordered and duplicates are dropped, missing ones are resent, and a window controls how much may be in flight. In 1978 the design was split into two layers, IP for forwarding packets between networks and TCP for reliable delivery on top.
CS032.analogy: Think of international post. A letter in a standard envelope crosses many countries’ postal systems, each only reading the address on the outside. The sender and receiver confirm that it arrived, so a lost letter can be sent again.
CS032.unlocked: TCP/IP became the language of the Internet: the ARPANET switched to it on 1 January 1983, and from there it spread to networks worldwide. Because it asked little of the networks beneath and carried any application above, the same design later carried email, the Web, streaming and everything else. Its open specification, developed in public, set a pattern for Internet standards. Cerf and Kahn received the Turing Award in 2004.
CS032.left_open: The first designs did not control congestion, and in 1986 the Internet suffered collapses that Van Jacobson’s algorithms fixed in 1988. Addresses were 32 bits, which ran short and led to IPv6. The protocol had no built-in security: packets could be forged or read in transit, which led to later layers such as TLS. And a design that assumes fixed machines on known networks fits mobility and strict timing guarantees poorly.
CS032.diagram_alt: A packet travelling from one host across three different networks joined by two gateways to a second host. Below, TCP at the two ends handles acknowledgement, ordering and resending, while IP forwards datagrams with network and host addresses.
review: ARPANET switched to TCP/IP on 1 January 1983 ('flag day'); the split into TCP and IP was in 1978
Van Jacobson's congestion control (1988) followed the 1986 collapses
Cerf and Kahn: Turing Award 2004

E067 and E068 (to End-to-end and to the Web proposal) are interpretive

CS033.problem: In the late 1960s the leading operating systems were huge and costly. IBM’s OS/360 had absorbed thousands of person-years, and Multics, a joint project of MIT, Bell Labs and General Electric, was ambitious and late; Bell Labs withdrew from it in 1969. Ken Thompson and Dennis Ritchie, who had worked on Multics, were left without a comfortable environment for programming. They wanted something small and pleasant that two people could understand and that ran on a cheap minicomputer, not a mainframe.
CS033.insight: UNIX was built on a few simple ideas applied consistently. Files are plain streams of bytes, arranged in a hierarchy of directories, and devices appear as files too, so the same read and write operations work on everything. Programs are small tools that each do one job and read and write text, and the pipe lets the output of one feed the input of the next, so tools can be combined into new ones without new code. The command interpreter, the shell, is just another program. New processes are created by a simple call, fork. In 1973 the system was rewritten in the C language, which made it portable to other machines.
CS033.analogy: It is a kitchen with a few good knives and bowls rather than one giant food machine. Because the tools fit together, you can make dishes the designers never imagined.
CS033.unlocked: UNIX became the ancestor of a whole family: BSD, System V, Linux, macOS and, through them, Android and iOS. Its ideas, files and pipes, small tools, the shell, process creation, remain the working vocabulary of programmers, and the C language grew up with it. Because the source was given to universities, it trained a generation of computer scientists, and Berkeley’s version carried the first widely used implementation of TCP/IP. Ritchie and Thompson received the Turing Award in 1983.
CS033.left_open: UNIX’s security model was simple: users, groups and permission bits, plus a trick that lets a program run with its owner’s rights, which later proved easy to abuse. Passing unstructured text between tools is flexible but forces every program to parse it. Networking, graphics and threads came later and less cleanly, and the many commercial variants fragmented the platform until standards such as POSIX. The system’s smallness, a virtue then, also meant much was left out.
CS033.diagram_alt: A pipeline of small programs, grep, sort and uniq, joined by pipes so each program's output feeds the next, beside a directory tree rooted at a single slash with bin, usr, dev and home. Everything, even devices, is a file.
review: The system was rewritten in C in 1973; the pipe was added in 1973 on McIlroy's proposal

CS034.problem: Large software projects were notoriously late and over budget, and managers had a standard answer: add more people. Fred Brooks had led the development of IBM’s OS/360 operating system, one of the largest and most troubled software projects of its time, and he had seen the cycle repeat. Projects were planned in “man-months,” as if people and months could be traded freely, and so schedules slipped further. Nobody had a good account of why software behaved differently from building a house or assembling a car.
CS034.insight: Brooks’s essays explain the pattern from experience. The man-month is a myth because work cannot be divided freely: some tasks are sequential, and each added person needs training and adds communication paths, which grow roughly with the square of the team size. So adding people to a late project makes it later, now called Brooks’s law. He argued that a system needs conceptual integrity, one coherent set of ideas, best secured by a small group of architects; recommended that small teams of specialists work like a surgical team; warned of the second-system effect, in which designers over-reach; and advised planning to throw the first version away.
CS034.analogy: Nine women cannot produce a baby in one month. Some jobs have a fixed length, and no amount of extra staff changes it; and a large kitchen of cooks may spend more time talking than cooking.
CS034.unlocked: The book became the most widely read work on software project management. “Adding manpower to a late project makes it later” is quoted constantly, and its themes of conceptual integrity, small teams, communication overhead and the difficulty of estimation recur in later practice, from agile methods to the design of team structures. Its essay form made hard-won experience accessible, and a 1995 anniversary edition added new reflections. Brooks received the Turing Award in 1999.
CS034.left_open: The rule of thumb is based on one large project and Brooks’s observation, not on controlled studies, and there are exceptions, for example when a project is in a phase that parallelises well. Some of his advice, such as planning to throw one version away, was revised by Brooks himself in favour of growing a system incrementally. The surgical team is hard to staff in practice. And the book was written for in-house development by large organisations, before open-source communities, distributed teams and modern tools changed how software is made.
CS034.diagram_alt: A schematic chart of time to finish against number of workers. The ideal curve falls steadily if work were perfectly divisible, but the real curve falls, bottoms out, then rises again as communication and training overhead grow, so more people make the project later.
review: Brooks managed OS/360 development at IBM; Turing Award 1999; anniversary edition 1995
Communication paths grow as n(n-1)/2 for a team of n
In the 1995 edition Brooks revised his advice to plan to throw one away in favour of incremental development

CS035.problem: Multi-user computers kept many people’s data and programs in one machine, and the machine had to stop them from reading or damaging one another’s information. By the mid-1970s, building such protection was mostly a matter of ad hoc fixes: added to systems after the fact, tested by trying to break in, with no shared vocabulary for what protection even meant or how to judge whether a design was sound. Saltzer and Schroeder, who had worked on the protection of the Multics system, set out to give the field principles.
CS035.insight: The paper surveys the mechanisms of protection, such as descriptors, access control lists, which attach to each object a list of who may use it, and capabilities, which are tickets held by users, and distils eight design principles for any protection system. Economy of mechanism: keep it small and simple. Fail-safe defaults: base access on permission rather than exclusion, so by default nobody is allowed. Complete mediation: check every access. Open design: security should not depend on the design being secret. Separation of privilege, least privilege, least common mechanism and psychological acceptability complete the list.
CS035.analogy: Think of a building. Give each person keys only to the rooms they need, lock every door by default, check badges at every door and not just at the front, and assume a burglar knows the floor plan.
CS035.unlocked: The principles became the standard vocabulary of security engineering and are still taught. Least privilege and default deny underlie modern operating systems, containers, sandboxes and firewalls; open design is the reason cryptographic algorithms are published and tested in public. Later security evaluation standards drew on them, and the debate it describes between access control lists and capabilities continues in system design. The paper also distinguished between protection mechanisms and the policies they enforce.
CS035.left_open: The principles are guidelines, not proofs of security, and they pull against each other: simplicity may conflict with checking everything, and strong separation may make a system hard to use. The paper treats a single computer with a trusted core; networks, malicious software, human error and the economics of attacks came to dominate. Cryptography is only briefly treated, and the paper does not say how to measure whether a design is actually secure.
CS035.diagram_alt: The eight design principles for protection systems shown as labelled tiles: economy of mechanism, fail-safe defaults, complete mediation, open design, separation of privilege, least privilege, least common mechanism and psychological acceptability. Fail-safe defaults is highlighted with the note default is deny.

CS036.problem: In 1975 computer science was still working out what kind of subject it was. Was it mathematics, engineering, or something else? And artificial intelligence faced doubters who said that machines could never think, and that programs were mere calculators. Allen Newell and Herbert Simon, who had built some of the first programs that solved problems that seemed to need intelligence, wanted to say what their work showed, about the machines and about the mind.
CS036.insight: In their joint Turing Award lecture they argued that computer science is an empirical science: programs and machines are real objects that behave in ways we do not always foresee, and we learn about them by building them and watching what they do, as other sciences do experiments. They stated two hypotheses. The physical symbol system hypothesis says that a system that manipulates symbols, structures built from them and processes that transform them has what is necessary and sufficient for general intelligent action. The heuristic search hypothesis says that problem-solving is search through a space of symbol structures, made feasible by rules of thumb that guide it toward solutions. Their evidence was a series of programs, from the Logic Theorist to chess players.
CS036.analogy: Think of an explorer in a vast maze. Trying every path would take forever, so the explorer follows hunches about which turns look promising. Newell and Simon said intelligence is that kind of guided exploration, in a space of symbols.
CS036.unlocked: The lecture gave symbolic AI its creed and cognitive psychology the idea that the mind can be studied as an information-processing system. It supported decades of work on search, planning, game playing and expert systems, with algorithms such as A* and game-tree search, and built the case that computing needs experiment as well as proof. Newell and Simon shared the 1975 Turing Award, and Simon later received a Nobel Prize in economics.
CS036.left_open: The hypotheses were contested from the start. Critics argued that intelligence depends on bodies, perception and learning from experience, which symbol manipulation neglects, and that symbols need to be tied to the world to mean anything. Neural networks, which learn patterns from data rather than following explicit rules and search, later achieved much of what symbolic AI struggled with. Whether the symbol-system claim is true, or merely a useful approximation, remains argued over.
CS036.diagram_alt: On the left, the three ingredients of a physical symbol system: symbols, expressions built from them and processes that transform them. On the right, a search tree in which unpromising branches are crossed out and a heuristically chosen path leads to the goal.
review: Newell and Simon received the 1975 Turing Award; the lecture was published in 1976; Simon won the 1978 Nobel Prize in economics
The two named hypotheses are the Physical Symbol System Hypothesis and the Heuristic Search Hypothesis

CS037.problem: Secret messages had always required the sender and receiver to share a secret key beforehand, which had to be delivered by a safe route, such as a courier. As computers and networks spread in the 1970s, that was a serious obstacle: a network of a thousand people would need hundreds of thousands of pairs of keys, each exchanged in advance. And while a handwritten signature proves who wrote a paper contract, there was nothing equivalent for messages sent electronically. Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman saw that cryptography had to change if it was to serve open networks.
CS037.insight: Their paper proposed two ideas. The first is public-key cryptography: each person has a pair of keys, one made public so anyone can use it to encrypt a message to them, and one kept private, which alone can decrypt it, so no secret needs to be shared in advance. The second is the digital signature: using one’s private key to produce something that anyone can verify with the public key, but nobody else could have produced. They also described a way, now called Diffie–Hellman key exchange, for two people to agree on a shared secret over a public channel, using the fact that raising a number to a power modulo a prime is easy, while recovering the power is believed to be hard.
CS037.analogy: Two people each pick a private paint colour, mix it with a common yellow, and swap the mixtures in public. Each then adds their own private colour to the mixture received, and both end up with the same final colour. Anyone watching sees only mixtures, which cannot be unmixed.
CS037.unlocked: Public-key cryptography is the basis of security on the Internet: key exchange of the Diffie–Hellman kind and digital signatures protect web browsing, secure shell, email, software updates and payments. Digital certificates, the way browsers know whose website they are talking to, are built on signatures. The paper also opened cryptography to academic research, outside the secrecy of governments, which was contentious at the time. Diffie and Hellman received the Turing Award in 2015.
CS037.left_open: The paper described the concept but did not have a practical public-key encryption method; that came two years later with RSA. Security rests on problems, such as discrete logarithms, that are only believed to be hard, and quantum computers could break them. Key exchange alone does not tell you who you are talking to, so an attacker in the middle could impersonate each side; authentication needs certificates or other trust. And the practical protocols took years of work to get right.
CS037.diagram_alt: A paint-mixing picture of key exchange. Alice and Bob each keep a private colour and mix it with a shared common colour, swap the mixtures in public, then each adds their own private colour to the mixture received. Both end with the same secret colour that an eavesdropper cannot recreate.
review: Diffie-Hellman Turing Award 2015; the paper also credits Merkle's work on puzzles
GCHQ researchers (Ellis, Cocks, Williamson) discovered similar ideas earlier in secret, declassified in 1997 (not mentioned in the text)
E061 (Cook to Diffie-Hellman) and E076 (Shannon to Diffie-Hellman) are interpretive; E075 (to RSA) is tagged explicit
The paint-mixing picture is a standard analogy, not the paper's own

CS038.problem: Alan Kay imagined the Dynabook: a portable personal computer, as easy to carry as a book, which children and adults could use to read, draw, make music, run simulations, and write their own programs. At Xerox PARC in the early 1970s the first Alto personal computers, with bitmap displays and a mouse, offered a chance to build something like it. But the existing languages, such as FORTRAN, BASIC and LISP, were made for experts or for calculation, and were awkward for creating interactive pictures and simulations. Kay wanted a language simple enough for a child to start with, and powerful enough for an adult to build a whole system.
CS038.insight: Smalltalk’s central idea is that a program is a society of objects that communicate by sending each other messages. Each object has its own state and decides how to respond to a message; you do not reach into it. This one idea replaces data structures, procedures and much else, so the language can be defined in a few pages. Kay drew on the object and class ideas of Simula, on the simplicity of LISP, on Sketchpad’s direct manipulation and on the children’s language Logo. The manual describes the 1972 version, in which each object parses the message it receives. Smalltalk was also an entire environment: windows, a mouse, and tools for editing and browsing code, all written in Smalltalk itself.
CS038.analogy: Imagine a town of small helpers who each know how to do certain tasks. To get something done you do not do it yourself; you send a note to the right helper, who decides how to carry it out.
CS038.unlocked: Smalltalk shaped object-oriented programming through its later versions, which influenced Objective-C, Java, Ruby and Python, and gave the world the graphical user interface with overlapping windows and menus, which Apple and Microsoft built on after Steve Jobs’s visit to PARC. Its programming environment prefigured modern development tools, and the Smalltalk community produced many ideas, such as the model-view-controller pattern, refactoring and design patterns. Alan Kay received the Turing Award in 2003.
CS038.left_open: Smalltalk-72 was an experimental language that was soon replaced by versions with classes and inheritance, so the manual records an early stage of the idea. Smalltalk ran slowly on the hardware of the time and it never won the market against languages that were faster and easier to fit into existing systems. Pure everything-is-an-object designs trade away some practicality, and inheritance, as later used, often produced tangled hierarchies. The Dynabook’s promise, a personal medium that children learn to program, has been only partly realised.
CS038.diagram_alt: Four objects, a window, a pen, a number and a menu, exchanging labelled messages such as draw, move by 10 and plus 4, beside a sketch of overlapping windows. Computation is objects sending messages to one another.
review: Smalltalk-72 manual edited by Goldberg and Kay (Xerox PARC, 1976); Kay: Turing Award 2003
Kay's credit to Simula, LISP, Sketchpad and Logo as influences comes from his own later accounts (basis for E072, E073, E035; all interpretive)
Steve Jobs's 1979 visit to Xerox PARC
E074 (Smalltalk to Design Patterns) is tagged explicit: the book draws on Smalltalk and MVC; verify

CS039.problem: In the mid-1970s there were several competing ways to describe the structure of a database: the relational model with its tables, the network model with its linked records, and others. Each came with its own concepts and terminology, and a designer had to start by thinking in terms of those, rather than in terms of the thing being described: customers, orders and products. The result was that databases were designed to fit the technology instead of the real world, and the people who knew the business could not easily read or check the design.
CS039.insight: Peter Chen proposed a simple way of thinking that comes before any of the models. The world is made of entities, things that can be told apart, such as an employee or a department; relationships among them, such as an employee works in a department; and attributes that describe them, such as a name or a salary. The model is drawn as a diagram, with boxes for entities and diamonds for relationships, and each relationship has a cardinality: one-to-one, one-to-many or many-to-many. This diagram could then be translated into tables, network structures or whatever the chosen system required. Chen called it a unified view of data, because it captured what the other models were trying to express.
CS039.analogy: It is the architect’s blueprint drawn before any bricks are chosen. You sketch the rooms and doors and how they connect, argue with the client over it, and only then decide whether to build in brick or timber.
CS039.unlocked: Entity-relationship diagrams became the standard way to design databases: nearly every database course teaches them and many design tools draw them. They separate conceptual design, what the business needs, from the logical and physical design that follows, a division still used in practice. The idea also influenced class diagrams in object-oriented design and modelling languages such as UML, and gave non-specialists a way to take part in design.
CS039.left_open: Chen’s original notation was extended many times, and today there are many incompatible drawing styles. The model describes structure but not behaviour or rules, and does not handle time well. Turning a diagram into tables raises choices, especially for many-to-many relationships, that the model does not settle, and deciding whether something is an entity or an attribute is a matter of judgment. Document and graph databases later dropped the fixed structure it presumes.
CS039.diagram_alt: An entity-relationship diagram: an Employee entity with attributes name and salary, joined through a works-in relationship diamond to a Department entity with attributes name and location, with many employees to one department.
review: Chen's paper appeared in ACM Transactions on Database Systems, 1976
Chen discusses the relational and network models and cites Codd (basis for E058, tagged explicit)
Influence on UML class diagrams is a common account, not a claim from Chen's paper

CS040.problem: Diffie and Hellman had proposed public-key cryptography in 1976, but they had not found a way to do it. They needed a trapdoor function: easy for anyone to compute, practically impossible to reverse unless you know a secret, the trapdoor. Without a concrete example the idea was just an idea, and it was not clear one existed. Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir and Leonard Adleman, at MIT, set out to find one, and also to make the signature idea of the 1976 paper work.
CS040.insight: Their answer came from number theory. Choose two large prime numbers, p and q, and publish their product n together with a number e. To send a message, treat it as a number m and compute m raised to the power e, modulo n. To decrypt, the owner uses a second number d, computed from p and q by a result of Euler, and raises the ciphertext to the power d modulo n, getting m back. Anyone can encrypt, but decrypting needs d, and working out d from n alone seems to require factoring n into p and q, which for large numbers nobody knew how to do quickly. Running the process in reverse, with the private key, gives a signature anyone can check.
CS040.analogy: Multiplying two large primes is like baking a cake: easy. Recovering the two primes from the product is like un-baking it. The public key is an open padlock anyone can snap shut; only the holder has the key to open it.
CS040.unlocked: RSA made public-key cryptography practical, and it was soon at the centre of secure communication: HTTPS certificates, signed software, email encryption such as PGP, secure shell and smart cards. It underpinned e-commerce by letting strangers establish trust. The inventors founded RSA Security and received the Turing Award in 2002. The paper also established the format of a cryptosystem whose security rests on a precisely stated mathematical problem, which opened modern cryptography to public scrutiny.
CS040.left_open: RSA’s security rests on the belief that factoring is hard, which is unproven; a fast factoring method, or a large quantum computer running Shor’s algorithm, would break it. Key sizes have had to grow as computers improved. The arithmetic is slow, so in practice RSA protects short secrets, such as the key for a faster cipher, and signs hashes. The plain form described in the paper is insecure without careful padding, and implementation flaws, such as timing leaks, have been a continuing source of attacks.
CS040.diagram_alt: A worked example with small numbers: primes 61 and 53 give n = 3233, with public exponent 17 and private exponent 2753. The message 65 encrypts to 2790 and decrypts back to 65. Multiplying primes is easy; factoring the product is believed hard.
review: The worked example (p=61, q=53, e=17, d=2753, m=65, c=2790) is the standard textbook example and was computed and checked, not taken from the paper
Rivest, Shamir and Adleman: Turing Award 2002; RSA Security was founded in 1982
GCHQ's Clifford Cocks found an equivalent scheme earlier in secret (declassified 1997)
E075 (Diffie-Hellman to RSA) is tagged explicit: the RSA paper cites 'New Directions'

CS041.problem: System programs such as operating systems were written in assembly language, which tied them to one machine and made them slow to write and hard to move. High-level languages like PL/I and ALGOL were too large and too inefficient for the job. At Bell Labs, UNIX had begun in assembly on the PDP-7 and PDP-11, and the earlier languages BCPL and B, which had no types, handled badly the byte-oriented PDP-11. Thompson and Ritchie wanted a language that could replace assembly language for systems work without giving up efficiency or control of the machine.
CS041.insight: Dennis Ritchie’s C was small and close to the machine while still being a real high-level language. Programs use types such as characters, integers and floating-point numbers, and structures that group data. Pointers, which hold addresses, are closely tied to arrays, so that working through memory is natural and efficient. Control structures are the structured ones Dijkstra argued for, and functions are the unit of program structure. Input and output are not built into the language but provided by a small library, so the language itself is easily moved to a new machine. Brian Kernighan and Ritchie’s book, a compact tutorial and reference, defined the language in practice, and its first example, a program that prints “hello, world”, became a tradition.
CS041.analogy: C is like a manual gearbox in a car: it gives you direct control over the machine and efficiency in return for care. If you are not careful you can stall, or damage the engine.
CS041.unlocked: C became the main language of systems programming. UNIX was rewritten in it, and so, in time, were Linux, the kernels of Windows and macOS, databases, compilers and embedded software. It was a base for later languages, C++, Objective-C, Java, C# and Go among them, and the book remained the standard description until ANSI C in 1989. Its portability showed that an operating system could be moved between machines by recompiling it.
CS041.left_open: C trusts the programmer. Nothing stops code from reading or writing beyond the end of an array or using memory after it is freed, and such memory-safety errors have caused a large share of serious security vulnerabilities for decades. Some behaviour is left undefined, so programs may behave differently across compilers. The language has no modules or namespaces, and little help for building large programs. Later languages, such as Java, Go and Rust, were designed in part to fix these problems.
CS041.diagram_alt: The classic hello world program in C on the left, and on the right a row of memory cells holding an array with a pointer that holds the address of the third cell, showing how C works close to the machine while staying portable by recompiling.
review: C descends from BCPL and B; the language was designed for UNIX (basis for E070, tagged explicit)
The 1978 book's first example prints 'hello, world'
ANSI C was standardised in 1989
E086 (ALGOL 60 to C) is interpretive: C's block structure and control flow descend from ALGOL through BCPL and B

CS042.problem: In a distributed system, programs run on different computers and communicate only by sending messages that take unpredictable time. There is no shared clock. Yet many problems need to know the order of events: which request came first, who should get a resource, whether one update could have affected another. Physical clocks on different machines drift apart and cannot be perfectly synchronised, so timestamps from them cannot be trusted to settle the order. Leslie Lamport asked what “before” should even mean for such a system.
CS042.insight: Lamport defined a happened-before relation. If two events are in the same process, the earlier one happened before the later; a message’s sending happens before its receipt; and the relation is transitive. Events not ordered by this are concurrent: neither could have influenced the other. He then gave a simple scheme, now called Lamport clocks: each process keeps a counter, increases it for every event, stamps messages with it, and, on receiving a message, moves its own counter past the stamp. The stamps never contradict happened-before. Breaking ties by process number yields one order for all events, which lets processes agree on, say, who has a lock, if each follows the same rules. He also showed how any service can be replicated by having each copy apply the same commands in the same order.
CS042.analogy: Think of pen-pals writing letters. Your reply certainly came after the letter you received, whatever the postmarks say. Two letters sent at the same time by different people have no natural order, and you only need a consistent way to choose one.
CS042.unlocked: The paper is one of the founding documents of distributed computing. Its ideas of causality and logical time gave rise to vector clocks, used to track versions in systems such as Dynamo, to state machine replication, which underlies consensus algorithms such as Paxos and Raft, and to tools that trace requests through large services. It changed how people reason about concurrency, by focusing on what can causally affect what. Lamport received the Turing Award in 2013.
CS042.left_open: The order logical clocks give can disagree with the real-time order users see, which causes surprising anomalies unless more is done. Producing a total order requires coordination, which costs time. The paper assumes processes do not fail, which real machines do and sometimes badly, which is the problem the Byzantine generals paper took up four years later. And later systems, such as Google’s Spanner, found it valuable to bring physical time back, with well-synchronised clocks.
CS042.diagram_alt: Three process timelines with events labelled by their logical clock values and two messages between them. A chain of happened-before links runs from the first event to the last, while two events with the same stamp on different processes are concurrent.
review: Lamport: Turing Award 2013
The 1978 paper's state-machine idea underlies Paxos and Raft; the Paxos paper cites it (E083 is tagged interpretive until checked)
Vector clocks were developed by Fidge and Mattern (1988) as a refinement
E055 (THE to Lamport, new domain), E082, E083 and E084 are interpretive

CS043.problem: The relational model promised that users could say what data they wanted in a high-level language, SQL, and leave the system to work out how. But that promise is only worth anything if the system does choose well. Even a simple query touching two or three tables can be run in many ways: using an index or scanning the whole table, joining tables in different orders, with different join methods. The cost of the best and worst can differ by factors of thousands. Critics argued that hand-tuned programs that navigated records would always beat a relational system.
CS043.insight: The IBM research team building the System R prototype, led here by Patricia Selinger, designed an optimizer that treats the choice as a cost estimation problem. It enumerates the ways to answer the query, estimates each plan’s cost from simple statistics kept about the tables and indexes, such as sizes and the number of distinct values, combining the expected disk reads and processor work, and picks the cheapest. To handle joins of many tables without trying every order, it uses dynamic programming: it finds the best plan for each smaller set of tables and builds up, keeping also plans that deliver rows in a useful order. Because the plan is chosen before running, the work is done once.
CS043.analogy: It is like a route planner. To get from A to B it estimates the time of each candidate route using what it knows about road lengths and traffic, and picks the quickest, rather than leaving the driver to guess.
CS043.unlocked: This paper is the template for the query optimizer in nearly every relational database, including Oracle, DB2, SQL Server and PostgreSQL. Cost-based optimisation made declarative SQL fast enough to win the market against hand-coded navigation, which finished the case for the relational model. Its ideas of statistics, selectivity estimates and join ordering by dynamic programming are still taught and used. System R also pioneered much else, including SQL itself, transactions and recovery, which became the DB2 product.
CS043.left_open: Cost estimates are only as good as the statistics, which are often wrong when columns are correlated or data is skewed, leading to terrible plans that are hard to diagnose. The number of possible plans grows explosively, so real optimizers rely on heuristics and give up on exhaustive search for big queries. The paper’s model assumed a single machine and a fixed plan: parallel and distributed systems, and plans that adapt as they run, needed later work, and learned estimates are an active research area.
CS043.diagram_alt: A query joining three tables A, B and C can be run as three different plans, each shown as a small join tree with an estimated cost: 1200, 340 and 900. The optimizer picks the cheapest, the middle plan.
review: System R was IBM Research's relational prototype at San Jose; the paper is by Selinger, Astrahan, Chamberlin, Lorie and Price
Dynamic programming over join orders and 'interesting orders' are the paper's key ideas
The costs in the diagram are illustrative
E059 (Codd to System R) is tagged explicit; E065 (B-trees to System R) and E085 (to shared nothing) are interpretive

CS044.problem: Concurrent programs, in which several processes run at once and share resources, are very hard to get right. Bugs depend on exactly how the processes happen to interleave, so they appear rarely, vanish when you look for them, and testing cannot find all of them. Proofs in the style of Hoare logic were possible, but for concurrent programs they were long, hard to find and easy to get wrong. Amir Pnueli had shown in 1977 that temporal logic, which talks about how things change over time, was a good language for stating what concurrent programs should do. But proving that a program satisfies such a statement still took ingenuity.
CS044.insight: Edmund Clarke and Allen Emerson, and independently Queille and Sifakis in France, realised that a great deal can be checked mechanically. A concurrent program with finitely many states can be described as a graph of states and moves between them, and a property written in temporal logic, such as “whenever a process requests the resource it eventually gets it,” can be checked by exploring that graph automatically. Clarke and Emerson used a branching-time logic, later called CTL, which can say things like “on all possible futures” and “on some future,” and gave an algorithm that checks a formula against a state graph in time proportional to the size of the graph and of the formula. Their paper also ran the idea backwards, building the synchronisation part of a program directly from its specification.
CS044.analogy: Instead of writing a mathematical proof that a maze has no dead end, you send a tireless explorer through every corridor and have it report any dead end it finds, together with the path that led there.
CS044.unlocked: This was the beginning of model checking, which turned verification from a task for experts into something a tool could do. If the property fails, the checker produces a counterexample, a concrete sequence of steps leading to the bug, which engineers find enormously useful. Model checking was later scaled up with symbolic methods and used on hardware designs, communication protocols and critical software, at companies such as Intel, Microsoft and Amazon. Clarke, Emerson and Sifakis received the Turing Award in 2007.
CS044.left_open: The central obstacle is state explosion: the number of states grows exponentially with the number of components, so even small systems can overwhelm the checker, and much later work, on symbolic representations, abstraction and reductions, fought this. The method checks a model of the system, not the code itself, so a wrong model gives false confidence. And it suits finite-state systems well but struggles with programs whose data is unbounded, where deductive proof remains necessary.
CS044.diagram_alt: A graph of program states with moves between them. A checker explores every state against a temporal logic formula, and when a property fails it reports the exact path of steps that leads to the bad state, shown in red, as a counterexample.
review: Clarke and Emerson 1981; Queille and Sifakis found the same idea independently; Turing Award 2007 (Clarke, Emerson, Sifakis)
Pnueli's 1977 paper introduced temporal logic for programs (basis for ghost G015 and edge E087, tagged explicit)
The logic in the paper is branching-time, later named CTL; the paper also synthesises synchronisation skeletons
E050 (Hoare logic to model checking) is interpretive

CS045.problem: A reliable computer system, such as the controls of an aircraft, is built from several computers that must agree on what to do, even if some of them fail. If a failed computer simply stops, the others can carry on. But failures can be worse: a faulty computer may send different, contradictory messages to different peers, or behave in ways nobody planned. Could a group of machines still reach agreement when some of them might actively mislead the rest? Nobody had a clear answer, or even a clear statement of the problem.
CS045.insight: Lamport, Shostak and Pease put the problem as a story: several divisions of the Byzantine army surround a city, each commanded by a general. The generals must agree on a common plan, attack or retreat, by messenger, but some may be traitors who send conflicting messages. They proved that, with spoken messages, agreement is possible only if more than two thirds of the generals are loyal: three generals cannot tolerate even one traitor, but four can, and in general 3m + 1 generals can tolerate m traitors. They gave algorithms that achieve it, and showed that if messages can be signed so that traitors cannot forge them, any number of traitors can be tolerated by the loyal generals.
CS045.analogy: Three people cannot agree reliably if one can lie: each hears conflicting stories and cannot tell who is lying. With four, the honest majority can compare notes, spot the inconsistency and outvote the liar.
CS045.unlocked: The paper defined what is now called Byzantine fault tolerance and the vocabulary of faulty, malicious and arbitrary behaviour. Its results guided the design of fault-tolerant computers for aircraft and spacecraft and of replicated systems in which some replicas may be compromised, and later practical algorithms such as Castro and Liskov’s PBFT. In the 2010s the same problem reappeared in blockchains, where participants do not trust each other. The result that 3m + 1 participants are needed to tolerate m traitors is still a basic fact of the field.
CS045.left_open: The algorithms assumed that messages are delivered reliably and within known time, and the early versions needed a number of messages that grows quickly with the number of generals. Real networks lose and delay messages, and a famous later result showed that agreement is impossible in a fully asynchronous system if even one process can crash. The paper gives a theory of agreement but little about building systems that are fast, which took decades of further work. And it assumes a fixed set of known participants.
CS045.diagram_alt: A commander sends attack to three lieutenants, one of whom is a traitor who tells another to retreat. The loyal lieutenants compare what they heard and agree by majority on attack. A note says that 3m + 1 generals can tolerate m traitors.
review: Authors of the paper: Lamport, Shostak and Pease (the CSV lists Lamport and Shostak)
With oral messages agreement needs more than two thirds loyal (n >= 3m+1); with signed messages any number of traitors can be tolerated
The impossibility result in asynchronous systems is Fischer, Lynch and Paterson (1985)
E082 (logical clocks to Byzantine generals) is interpretive; E088 (to Paxos) and E089 (to Bitcoin) are interpretive

CS046.problem: Designers of networked systems face a choice about where to put a function such as reliable delivery, error detection, encryption or the ordering of messages: in the network itself, or in the programs running at the ends. Putting every useful function in the network sounds helpful: if the network guarantees reliable delivery, applications need not worry. But a network that tries to do many things becomes complex, and its builders must guess what applications will need. By the early 1980s, with the Internet’s design under way, there was no clear principle for deciding.
CS046.insight: Jerome Saltzer, David Reed and David Clark argued that a function can be completely and correctly implemented only with the knowledge and help of the application at the ends of the communication, so providing it in the middle of the network may be only a performance enhancement. Their example is a file transfer. Even if every link along the way checks for errors, a fault in the disk or the software at either end could still corrupt the file, so the applications must check the whole file, end to end, anyway. A check by each hop is then redundant; it may help speed by catching errors early, but it cannot replace the check at the ends. So keep the network simple, and put functions at the ends unless the network can do them better for everyone.
CS046.analogy: Consider sending a valuable parcel. A courier may check the package at every depot, but the only check that really counts is the recipient opening it and confirming that everything is there. Extra checks along the way may find problems sooner, but they cannot replace the final one.
CS046.unlocked: The end-to-end argument became a guiding principle of Internet design: a simple, general network that moves packets, with intelligence at the edges. It made it possible to deploy new applications, from the Web to video calling, without asking permission from the network or changing it, and it shaped debates over network neutrality, where the question is whether the network should treat all packets alike.
CS046.left_open: The argument is a design heuristic, not a theorem. It says when to prefer the ends, not when to refuse the middle: there are cases, such as performance, security or congestion, where the network is the right place. Firewalls, caches and content networks now sit inside the network, bending the principle. It assumes the ends can be trusted, which is not so when they are controlled by attackers, or when the interests of users, network operators and governments differ. How much intelligence belongs in the network remains an arguable question.
CS046.diagram_alt: A file travelling from one host through three network hops to another host. Each hop has a small check, but a corruption introduced by software at the sending end passes them all; only an end-to-end check by the receiving application catches it.
review: Saltzer, Reed and Clark, 1984; the file-transfer example is the paper's own
The Internet's design philosophy is often cited as following this principle; E067 (TCP/IP to end-to-end) and E090 (end-to-end to the Web) are interpretive
Network neutrality as an application of the principle is a common account, not the paper's claim

CS047.problem: In the early 1980s, introductory programming courses mostly taught the syntax of a language and recipes for common tasks. Students learned to write programs but not what programs are: how large systems are controlled by building abstractions, what it means to compute, and how a language itself is built. At MIT, Harold Abelson and Gerald Jay Sussman wanted to teach computer science as the study of ideas for managing complexity, so that beginners could think like designers and not only like coders.
CS047.insight: Their textbook, taught with the Scheme dialect of LISP, built everything from a few ideas. Procedures can be passed around as values; data can be hidden behind abstractions, so that a program using a rational number does not need to know how it is represented; the same program can be viewed as an object with changing state or as a stream of values; and a language can be defined by writing its own interpreter. The central chapter has the reader write a metacircular evaluator, an interpreter for Scheme written in Scheme, and then other machines, including one that compiles it, so that the reader sees how a language works from the inside. Three methods run through the book: primitive building blocks, ways of combining them, and ways of abstracting what has been combined.
CS047.analogy: Most courses teach cooking by handing out recipes. This one teaches what cooking is, then asks the student to design a kitchen, and finally to build the stove too.
CS047.unlocked: SICP, often called the “wizard book,” trained a generation of programmers and shaped how computer science is taught: courses at many universities followed it, and its emphasis on abstraction, functional programming and interpreters seeded later languages and teaching ideas. The book made LISP’s ideas, such as higher-order functions and code as data, familiar to educators and fed into modern functional-style programming. It remains a favourite of those who think programming is a branch of thinking.
CS047.left_open: SICP is demanding for novices, and many departments moved toward more practical introductions; MIT itself replaced the course around 2008 with one using Python. Its tools, Scheme and a deliberate absence of types, and its focus on a single paradigm hide issues of large-scale engineering: teams, testing and changing requirements. Whether abstraction is best learned first, or after building simple things, remains argued over.
CS047.diagram_alt: Three methods of controlling complexity: primitive building blocks, means of combination and means of abstraction. A short Scheme definition of square sits beside an eval and apply loop, showing an interpreter written in the language it runs.
review: Taught at MIT as the introductory course (6.001); the course was replaced around 2007-08 by a Python-based one
The metacircular evaluator is in chapter 4; the register-machine compiler in chapter 5
E028 (LISP to SICP) is tagged explicit: the book is built on Scheme, a LISP dialect; E091 and E092 are interpretive

CS048.problem: Neural networks that learn were an old idea, and the perceptron of the late 1950s could learn to classify simple patterns. But a perceptron with only one layer of adjustable connections can learn only the simplest patterns, and Marvin Minsky and Seymour Papert’s 1969 book stressed these limits. Adding hidden layers between input and output would make a network far more powerful, but how could one train them? For a connection deep inside, nobody could tell how a change would affect the final error, so research in the area slowed for years.
CS048.insight: The paper presented backpropagation, a way to calculate, for every connection in a multilayer network, how much changing it would change the output error. The network is run forward on an example, the error at the output is measured, and then the error is passed backward through the network, layer by layer, using the chain rule of calculus to apportion blame to each connection. Each connection is then adjusted a little in the direction that reduces the error, a procedure called gradient descent. The authors showed that, trained this way, the hidden layers learned useful internal representations of the data, features that nobody had programmed in, on tasks such as encoding patterns and learning family relationships.
CS048.analogy: Imagine a company that makes a poor product. Backpropagation traces the complaint back from the customer through each department, working out how much each contributed, so that every team can adjust its own part a little.
CS048.unlocked: Backpropagation turned multilayer networks into practical learning machines. It drove the first wave of neural-network applications, such as handwriting recognition, and, after the 2000s brought large datasets and fast graphics processors, powered the deep-learning revolution from image recognition to language models. Almost every neural network today is trained with it. The paper’s emphasis on learned representations became a central idea in machine learning. Hinton, with Bengio and LeCun, received the Turing Award in 2018.
CS048.left_open: The idea was not entirely new, with earlier versions by Linnainmaa, Werbos and others; the 1986 paper’s impact lay in showing that it worked and in how it was presented. Training was slow, and deep networks suffered from vanishing gradients, so for much of the 1990s and 2000s other methods, such as support vector machines, did better. It needs large amounts of labelled data and computing. And the learned representations are hard to interpret, leaving open why networks work and when they fail.
CS048.diagram_alt: A small neural network with input, hidden and output layers. Blue arrows run forward to compute the output; red dashed arrows run backward carrying the error so that each connection can be adjusted a little to reduce it.
review: Rumelhart, Hinton and Williams, Nature 1986; Turing Award 2018 (Hinton, Bengio, LeCun)
Earlier versions: Linnainmaa 1970, Werbos 1974

CS049.problem: By the mid-1980s relational databases were popular, and customers wanted them to handle more data and more users than any single computer could. Building a parallel database meant choosing how the processors would be connected to memory and disks. One choice, shared memory, lets all processors use one memory, which is easy to program but hits a bottleneck as processors are added. Another, shared disk, lets every processor reach all the disks. Michael Stonebraker asked which architecture would scale best, and which could be built from affordable parts.
CS049.insight: Stonebraker compared three architectures and argued for the third: shared nothing, in which each processor has its own memory and its own disks, and the machines communicate only by sending messages over a network. Data is partitioned among the machines, and each works on its own part; queries are broken up and run in parallel, and the results combined. Because nothing is shared, there is no central memory or disk to become a bottleneck, so adding machines can add capacity almost in proportion, and the machines can be ordinary, cheap computers. Failures are contained, and given replicas the system can keep working if one node dies. The price is that data must be partitioned well and moved across the network when a query needs it.
CS049.analogy: Think of a supermarket. Rather than every shopper crowding through one door and one till, you open more shops, each with its own stock and staff, and give each shop its own set of customers. Adding shops handles more shoppers.
CS049.unlocked: Shared nothing became the dominant design for large-scale data systems. Commercial parallel databases such as Teradata used it, and so did the cloud-era systems that scale across thousands of commodity machines: Google’s storage and MapReduce, Hadoop, and many NoSQL and distributed SQL databases. It is why data warehouses can grow by adding nodes, and the vocabulary of partitions, shards and replicas descends from it.
CS049.left_open: Partitioning is the hard part: a poor split leaves some machines overloaded, and queries that need data from many partitions spend their time moving it. Adding or removing machines means redistributing data. Transactions that span nodes need protocols to commit together, which are costly. And the paper was a short argument with limited evidence; later systems showed that shared disk and shared memory can win in some settings, for example with fast networks and modern storage.
CS049.diagram_alt: Three parallel database architectures: shared memory, where processors share one memory; shared disk, where they share the disks; and shared nothing, where each node has its own processor, memory and disk and they communicate only over a network, so it scales by adding nodes.
review: Stonebraker's paper appeared in IEEE Database Engineering Bulletin, 1986
Teradata and later systems used the shared-nothing design

CS050.problem: By 1986 progress in hardware was spectacular: each year machines were faster and cheaper by large factors. Software had not kept pace, and every few years a new technique, a high-level language, structured programming, object-oriented programming, artificial intelligence, was promised to deliver a tenfold gain in productivity. Brooks, who had written about the troubles of large projects a decade earlier, asked whether any single new development could really give the order-of-magnitude improvement that managers hoped for.
CS050.insight: His essay distinguishes essential difficulties, those inherent in the nature of software, from accidental ones, those that come from the tools and techniques of the day. He argued that the essence is a construct of interlocking concepts, data sets, relationships, algorithms and calls, which is hard because of four properties: complexity, since software has enormous numbers of states and parts; conformity, since it must fit arbitrary human institutions and interfaces; changeability, since it is always asked to change; and invisibility, since it has no natural geometric form. Past breakthroughs, such as high-level languages, had removed accidental difficulties, and little of that kind was left. Hence, he predicted, no single development in technology or management technique would by itself bring a tenfold improvement within a decade.
CS050.analogy: Writing a book got easier when word processors replaced typewriters, but no tool makes the plot easier to invent. The hard part, deciding what to say, remains.
CS050.unlocked: The essay gave the field a durable way to talk about why software is hard, and a test to apply to every new miracle promise: does it attack the essential complexity, or only the accidental kind? Brooks recommended promising attacks that did: buying rather than building, rapid prototyping and incremental growth of systems, and growing great designers. These themes echo through agile methods, reuse, open source and modern advice. His prediction that nothing would give a tenfold gain in ten years has largely held, and the essay is still cited whenever a new tool is announced with big promises.
CS050.left_open: Critics argue that Brooks underrated the gains from reuse of software, open-source libraries and the cloud, which have sharply cut the work of building many applications, and that the division between essential and accidental is a matter of judgement. Whether a prediction about a decade held depends on how productivity is measured, which the essay does not settle. And it offers little guidance on how to make progress on the essential complexity beyond hoping for better designers and better ways of working.
CS050.diagram_alt: Software difficulty shown as a large block of essential difficulty, with its four properties complexity, conformity, changeability and invisibility, above a thin block of accidental difficulty that earlier tools had already shrunk. A note says no single silver bullet removes the essential part.
review: Brooks, 'No Silver Bullet: Essence and Accidents of Software Engineering', 1986/87 (the CSV lists 1987)
The four essential properties: complexity, conformity, changeability, invisibility
The 'promising attacks' he names include buy versus build, rapid prototyping, incremental development and growing great designers

CS051.problem: CERN, the European particle physics laboratory, had thousands of researchers who came and went, using many different computers and keeping information in many different formats, and its projects lasted years while people moved on. Documentation was lost, and finding who had done what, or which program depended on which, was hard. Existing systems organised information in a strict hierarchy, such as a directory tree, or in a central database, neither of which fitted the way the organisation really worked: as a web of links among people, projects and documents.
CS051.insight: Tim Berners-Lee’s proposal suggested a system of hypertext: documents linked to one another by links that readers could follow, not arranged in a fixed hierarchy. Anyone could add a document and link it to others without asking permission from a central authority, and the system would work across the different computers of the laboratory. His proposal sketched a network of nodes and links, with a browser to follow them. In 1990 he turned it into the World Wide Web, with three simple ingredients: a way to name any document, the URL; a protocol to fetch it, HTTP; and a markup language to write it, HTML. His manager’s note on the proposal is famous: “Vague but exciting.”
CS051.analogy: Think of the difference between a library arranged on strict shelves and an encyclopedia full of “see also” references. In the second, you follow your interest from one article to the next, and anyone can add another reference.
CS051.unlocked: The World Wide Web grew from this proposal. CERN placed the technology in the public domain in 1993, and with the Mosaic browser the Web spread explosively, turning the Internet from a tool for specialists into a global medium for publishing, commerce, social life and software delivery. Search engines such as Google’s grew out of its links. Berners-Lee later founded the World Wide Web Consortium to keep the standards open, and received the Turing Award in 2016.
CS051.left_open: The original Web was a read-mostly system of linked pages with no memory of the user and no way to ensure that links stay valid, so links break; the “404” became familiar. It had no built-in identity, privacy or security, which were added unevenly later, with consequences such as tracking, misinformation and large concentrations of power in a few platforms. Berners-Lee himself has been outspoken about these developments and has proposed projects to give people control of their own data. And the proposal’s vision of machines understanding the links, the Semantic Web, has only partly arrived.
CS051.diagram_alt: On the left a strict tree hierarchy of documents; on the right a web of documents joined by arbitrary links that anyone can add. Three ingredients are named: URL to name a document, HTTP to fetch it and HTML to write it.
review: The proposal was written at CERN in March 1989; the manager's 'Vague but exciting' note is from Mike Sendall (as widely reported)
CERN put the Web technology in the public domain in 1993; the Mosaic browser followed
Berners-Lee: Turing Award 2016

CS052.problem: Before 1990, computer architecture was often taught and practised as a matter of style and taste. Designers argued about instruction sets and features, such as complex instructions that mimicked high-level languages, on the basis of elegance and experience, without agreed measurements. Engineers had few ways to say, with evidence, whether a new feature was worth its cost. John Hennessy at Stanford and David Patterson at Berkeley, who had each led the design of experimental simple processors, believed that design should be driven by measurements of real programs.
CS052.insight: Their book recast architecture as an engineering discipline based on quantitative principles. It made explicit a handful of guidelines: make the common case fast, since improving what happens most is worth more than improving what is rare; use Amdahl’s law to bound the gain from any improvement; and write performance as the product of three things, the number of instructions, the cycles each takes and the length of a cycle, so that trade-offs can be analysed. It explained how to measure with benchmarks and to model and simulate designs, and used the measurements to explain why simple, regular instruction sets, the RISC approach, with pipelining and caches, beat complex ones. Each chapter presented design options with data on their cost and performance.
CS052.analogy: Think of tuning a delivery business. Rather than arguing about which vehicle looks best, you measure which routes are used most and speed those up, and you calculate how much any improvement can actually save.
CS052.unlocked: The book became the standard text and shaped a generation of designers. Its approach turned RISC from a research idea into the mainstream, ending most debate over complex instruction sets in new designs, and gave the field a common vocabulary and common benchmarks. It continued through many editions as the problems moved on to instruction-level parallelism, multicore, memory hierarchies, warehouse-scale computers and domain-specific accelerators. Hennessy and Patterson received the Turing Award in 2017.
CS052.left_open: Quantitative methods depend on the programs one chooses to measure, and a benchmark suite can mislead or be gamed. Designers can optimise what is measured at the expense of what is not. The book’s assumptions about technology trends, such as steady gains from smaller transistors, had to be revised when Dennard scaling ended and single-thread speed stopped improving, pushing the field toward parallelism and specialisation. And the methods suit incremental refinement better than the invention of new kinds of machine.
CS052.diagram_alt: The performance equation: execution time equals instruction count times cycles per instruction times seconds per cycle. Below, a bar of run time split into a large common case and a small rare case, with the note that speeding up the common case pays most.
review: Hennessy (Stanford, MIPS) and Patterson (Berkeley, RISC); Turing Award 2017
The three-factor performance equation and 'make the common case fast' are central to the book

CS053.problem: Object-oriented languages let programmers define a new type as a subtype of an existing one, and then use objects of the new type wherever the old was expected. But what should “subtype” mean? Most languages checked only that the new type had the right method names and signatures. That is not enough: a type can have all the right methods and still behave in ways that break programs written for the original, as a square class that inherits from a rectangle but cannot have its width and height changed independently. Programmers needed a rule for when substitution is safe.
CS053.insight: Barbara Liskov, who had long argued for data abstraction, and Jeannette Wing proposed a behavioural definition: an object of a subtype should be usable wherever an object of the supertype is expected, without a program written for the supertype noticing the difference. The substitution principle, which Liskov first stated in 1987, is made precise with specifications. The subtype’s methods must accept at least what the supertype’s methods accept, so preconditions may be no stronger, and promise at least what they promise, so postconditions may be no weaker. The subtype must also preserve the supertype’s invariants and its “history” properties, such as an immutable object staying unchanged. The paper gives rules, and a way to check them using abstraction functions that relate the subtype’s representation to the supertype’s.
CS053.analogy: If you hire a substitute pilot, you do not just check that they can fly. You need them to be able to do everything the original pilot was trusted to do, and not to do anything the airline’s procedures forbid.
CS053.unlocked: The Liskov substitution principle became the “L” in the SOLID principles of object-oriented design and one of the most quoted guidelines in programming: inheritance should model behaviour, not just shape. It underlies design by contract, the discipline of stating preconditions and postconditions for classes, and informs type-system rules such as the treatment of variance, and testing methods that check a subclass against its parent’s specification. Liskov received the Turing Award in 2008.
CS053.left_open: Checking behavioural subtyping needs complete specifications, which most programs lack, so in practice the principle guides design more than tools enforce it. Languages check only signatures, and common practices such as inheriting from a class merely to reuse its code ignore it. Mutable objects, aliasing and concurrency make the rules harder to apply. And a strict reading rules out some useful designs, so developers debate how literally to apply it.
CS053.diagram_alt: A Square type that inherits from Rectangle breaks code that sets width and height separately: expected area 20 but the square gives 25. The behavioural rules: preconditions no stronger, postconditions no weaker, invariants preserved.
review: Liskov and Wing, ACM TOPLAS 1994; the substitution principle was stated by Liskov in 1987; Liskov received the Turing Award in 2008
The square/rectangle example is the standard illustration, not the paper's own
