CS054.problem: Object-oriented programmers kept running into the same design problems and solving them again, with varying skill. Experienced designers knew solutions that worked, such as how to let many parts of a program react to a change without tying them to each other, but this knowledge lived in their heads and in particular programs. Beginners could learn the features of C++ or Smalltalk without learning how to use them to build flexible designs. There was no shared vocabulary for describing designs, and no catalogue of what good designers knew.
CS054.insight: Erich Gamma, Richard Helm, Ralph Johnson and John Vlissides, who became known as the Gang of Four, borrowed an idea from the architect Christopher Alexander: a pattern is a named, general solution to a recurring problem in a given context. Their book catalogued 23 of them for object-oriented software, grouped as creational, structural and behavioural, such as Observer, Factory, Adapter and Strategy. Each is described in the same way, with its intent, the problem it solves, a structure diagram, how the parts collaborate, the consequences and sample code. Behind them were two principles: program to an interface, not an implementation, and favour composing objects over inheriting from classes.
CS054.analogy: Think of the standard openings in chess, or a carpenter’s named joints. Once a joint has a name, an experienced builder can say “dovetail” and everyone knows its shape, its purpose and its trade-offs.
CS054.unlocked: The book gave programmers a shared vocabulary, so that “this is an Observer” conveys a whole design in a word, and it became one of the best-selling and most influential software books. It popularised the pattern idea in architecture reviews, frameworks and teaching, and inspired catalogues of patterns for other domains such as concurrency, enterprise systems and user interfaces. Its two principles shaped how object-oriented design is taught.
CS054.left_open: Critics argue that many patterns compensate for gaps in languages like C++ and Java, and that dynamic or functional languages need fewer of them: in effect, some patterns are missing language features. Treating the catalogue as a checklist led to over-engineered code with patterns applied for their own sake. The book’s examples reflect the C++ and Smalltalk of its day, and the claim that patterns improve designs has been hard to test empirically. Describing design in prose and diagrams is also less precise than formal specification.
CS054.diagram_alt: A pattern card with four parts, name, problem, solution and consequences, beside the Observer pattern: a subject notifies three observers whenever its state changes, without knowing what they do. A note credits the idea of patterns to Christopher Alexander's architecture.
review: Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides, 1994; 23 patterns in three groups
The book credits Christopher Alexander for the pattern idea (basis for ghost G014 and edge E102, tagged explicit)
E074 (Smalltalk to the book) is tagged explicit: the book draws on Smalltalk examples such as Model-View-Controller; E064 and E098 are interpretive

CS055.problem: By the early 1990s, machine learning faced a dilemma. Linear classifiers, which separate two classes with a straight line or flat surface, were well understood and had good guarantees, but real data is rarely separable that way. Multilayer neural networks could draw more complex boundaries, but they were hard to train: the training could get stuck in poor solutions, results depended on many choices, and it was hard to tell whether a trained network would work well on new data rather than just memorise its examples. Corinna Cortes and Vladimir Vapnik, at AT&T Bell Labs, wanted a method that was both flexible and backed by theory.
CS055.insight: Their support-vector network rests on two ideas. First, among all lines or planes that separate the classes, choose the one with the largest margin, the widest empty gap between the classes. Only the few training points closest to the boundary, the support vectors, determine it, which keeps the solution simple and, as Vapnik’s statistical learning theory shows, helps it generalise to new data. Second, to handle data that is not linearly separable, map it into a space of many more dimensions where a flat boundary can work, without ever computing that mapping, by using a kernel function that gives the inner products directly. Training is a convex optimisation problem, so it has one best answer and no poor local solutions. A soft-margin version tolerates some errors.
CS055.analogy: To separate two crowds in a hall with a rope, you do not stretch it just anywhere; you lay it down the middle of the widest empty corridor, as far as possible from both crowds, and only the people standing nearest the rope matter.
CS055.unlocked: Support vector machines became the leading general-purpose learning method of the late 1990s and 2000s, applied to handwriting recognition, text classification, bioinformatics and many other problems, often with excellent results from modest amounts of data. The kernel trick spread across statistics and machine learning, and the paper helped bring statistical learning theory and optimisation into mainstream practice. Together with boosting and random forests, they defined the era in which deep networks were out of fashion.
CS055.left_open: Training cost grows quickly with the number of examples, which limits SVMs on very large datasets. The choice of kernel and its parameters matters and needs care, and the method does not learn features: the data’s representation is chosen by hand or by the kernel. When large datasets and graphics processors made deep networks trainable in the 2010s, networks that learn their own features overtook SVMs on images and speech, though SVMs remain useful on smaller problems.
CS055.diagram_alt: Two classes of points separated by a line placed in the middle of the widest empty margin. Only the few points touching the margin, the support vectors, determine the line. A note says a kernel lifts non-separable data so a flat boundary can work.
review: Cortes and Vapnik, Machine Learning 1995; the kernel idea goes back to Boser, Guyon and Vapnik (1992)
The soft-margin formulation is introduced in this paper
E104 (Perceptron to SVM) and E105 (backpropagation as the rival) are interpretive

CS056.problem: Most machine learning needs a teacher who supplies the right answer for each example. But much of what living things learn comes from consequences: a child learns to ride a bicycle by wobbling and falling, an animal learns where food is found. In such problems no one tells the learner what the correct action was; it gets only a reward or penalty, often long after the action that earned it. By the 1990s there were scattered methods for this, from psychology, control theory, dynamic programming and artificial intelligence, but no unified framework or standard account.
CS056.insight: Richard Sutton and Andrew Barto’s book gave that account. An agent interacts with an environment: at each step it observes a state, chooses an action, and receives a reward and a new state. Its goal is to choose actions that maximise the total reward over time. The central tools are value functions, which estimate how good it is to be in a state or to take an action, and the Bellman equations that relate the value of a state to that of its successors. Methods include dynamic programming when the rules are known; Monte Carlo methods, which learn from complete episodes; and temporal-difference learning, which learns guesses from other guesses and updates after every step. A recurring tension is between exploiting what works and exploring to find something better.
CS056.analogy: Learning to play a new game without a rulebook or coach. You try moves, notice that some lead to winning positions and others to losing ones, and gradually learn which positions are worth steering towards.
CS056.unlocked: The book unified the field and trained a generation of researchers, and its vocabulary of agents, rewards, value functions and policies is now standard. The ideas, joined with deep neural networks, produced systems that mastered Atari games, the game of Go in AlphaGo, and robot control, and a form of reinforcement learning from human feedback is used to tune large language models. The framework also connects to neuroscience, where dopamine signals resemble temporal-difference errors.
CS056.left_open: Reinforcement learning is data-hungry: agents often need millions of trials, which is affordable in a simulator but not in a hospital or a factory. Designing the reward is hard, and an agent may find unintended ways to earn it. Learning is unstable when functions are approximated by networks, and what is learned in one setting often fails to carry to another. The book’s first edition treats mostly small, tabular problems, and the harder question of scaling to the real world was left open.
CS056.diagram_alt: An agent and an environment in a loop: the agent sends an action, and the environment returns a new state and a reward. Three families of methods are named below: dynamic programming, Monte Carlo and temporal-difference learning.
review: Sutton and Barto, first edition 1998 (MIT Press)
Dopamine neurons and temporal-difference errors: Schultz, Dayan and Montague (1997)
The reinforcement-learning-from-human-feedback remark relates to later practice, not to the book

CS057.problem: By 1997 the Web held tens of millions of pages and was growing explosively, and finding anything was a problem. The existing search engines matched the words in a query against the text of pages, and ranked results mostly by how often and where the words appeared. Such rankings were easy to manipulate: a page could repeat its keywords, and the results were often poor. Sergey Brin and Larry Page, then PhD students at Stanford, believed that the structure of the Web, which pages link to which, contained information that was being ignored.
CS057.insight: Their key idea was PageRank. A link from one page to another is a kind of vote, and votes from important pages count for more. A page’s importance is therefore defined in terms of the importance of the pages that link to it, a circular definition that can be solved: it is the probability that a “random surfer” who keeps following links at random, occasionally jumping to a random page, is on that page at any moment, and it can be computed by repeating a simple calculation over the link graph until it settles. Google combined it with the text of the links pointing to a page, called anchor text, and with careful use of the page’s own text and formatting. The paper also described in detail how to crawl, index and search hundreds of millions of pages on commodity machines.
CS057.analogy: Think of academic citations. A paper cited by many well-cited papers is probably important, and a citation from a famous paper is worth more than one from an unknown one.
CS057.unlocked: PageRank and the system built around it produced noticeably better results than competitors and made Google the dominant search engine. Link analysis changed the Web: it created the industry of search engine optimisation and led to spam and countermeasures. The Google infrastructure the paper sketched drove the company’s later work on distributed storage and processing, and the idea of ranking by network structure was applied to citations, social networks and recommendation.
CS057.left_open: Links can be bought, faked or farmed, and ranking by popularity can favour what is already popular. A single importance score for each page ignores the query and the person asking. The paper itself warns that advertising-funded search engines may be biased toward advertisers, and raises worries about scale and about the privacy of search logs; these concerns remained. And the original algorithm is now only one signal among many in a modern ranking system.
CS057.diagram_alt: A small web of pages joined by links. Each page is drawn with a size proportional to its PageRank, so pages that receive links from other important pages are larger. A note says a link is a vote and votes from important pages count more.
review: Brin and Page, WWW7 conference 1998; the paper's appendix on advertising and mixed motives
The PageRank values in the diagram were computed for the small example graph (damping 0.85), not taken from the paper

CS058.problem: Distributed systems often need several machines to agree on a single value, such as which operation comes next in a log, even though machines can crash and restart, and messages can be delayed, lost or duplicated. This is the consensus problem. A 1985 result by Fischer, Lynch and Paterson had shown that no algorithm can guarantee agreement in an asynchronous system if even one machine can fail, so any practical solution would have to give up something. By the late 1980s, protocols for replicated databases were complex, and it was hard to know whether any of them was correct.
CS058.insight: Lamport’s paper describes Paxos, an algorithm that is always safe, never choosing two different values even if machines fail and messages are lost, and that makes progress whenever a majority of machines can communicate. To make the idea memorable he told it as the story of the legislators of the Greek island of Paxos, who decide laws although they come and go from the chamber. A value is chosen in two phases. First a proposer asks a majority of acceptors to promise not to accept older proposals and reports any value they may already have accepted; then, if a majority promises, it proposes a value, which must be the one already accepted if there is one, and when a majority accepts it, it is chosen. Because any two majorities overlap, a chosen value can never be lost.
CS058.analogy: Imagine a council that must agree on one decree, though members wander in and out. A member proposing a decree first checks with a majority whether any decree may already have been agreed, and if so adopts it. Because any two majorities share a member, a decision, once made, cannot be silently overturned.
CS058.unlocked: Paxos became the basis for fault-tolerant services at the core of large systems: Google’s Chubby lock service, Spanner and many others use it, and it is the model for later algorithms for replicated state machines. It showed how to replicate a service by agreeing on the order of its commands, the state machine approach from Lamport’s 1978 paper. Lamport received the Turing Award in 2013, in part for this work. Consensus became a standard building block of reliable infrastructure.
CS058.left_open: Paxos is famously hard to understand. The paper’s allegory baffled reviewers, and it sat unpublished for years until the journal printed it in 1998; even after Lamport’s later plain-language description, engineers found it hard to turn into a complete system, since the single-decision algorithm omits leader election, log management and reconfiguration. Those difficulties led directly to alternatives such as Raft, designed for understandability. And it tolerates crashes, not malicious faults.
CS058.diagram_alt: A proposer and three acceptors in two phases. In phase one the proposer sends prepare and a majority of acceptors answer with promises. In phase two it sends accept and a majority accepts. Any two majorities overlap, so a chosen value is never lost.
review: Lamport wrote the paper in 1989-90; it was published in ACM TOCS in 1998; the Fischer-Lynch-Paterson impossibility result is 1985
Chubby (Google's lock service) and Spanner use Paxos (basis for E110, Paxos to Spanner, tagged explicit)
E109 (Paxos to Raft) is tagged explicit: Raft's stated aim is to be easier to understand than Paxos; E083 and E088 are interpretive

CS059.problem: In the 1990s, most software was built following heavy, plan-driven processes: gather all the requirements, design the whole system, then code, then test. The assumption was that changing the software late costs enormously more than changing it early, so one must get everything right in advance. But requirements kept changing, projects ran late, and the paperwork often felt like a burden rather than a help. Kent Beck, working on a payroll project at Chrysler, wondered what would happen if you took the practices that seemed to work, and turned them all up to the maximum.
CS059.insight: Extreme Programming, or XP, is a small set of practices based on the values of communication, simplicity, feedback, courage and respect. Programmers work in pairs; they write automated tests before the code that satisfies them, which is test-driven development; they build the system in very small releases, integrating and testing many times a day; they keep the design simple and continually improve it, a practice called refactoring; the customer sits with the team and decides priorities through short “user stories”; and the team plans in short iterations. The practices support each other: tests make refactoring safe, and refactoring keeps the design simple, which keeps change cheap. Beck’s bet was that, with these practices, the cost of changing software would stay low rather than rise steeply.
CS059.analogy: It is like steering a boat by constant small corrections rather than plotting a perfect course at the start: you look often, adjust a little, and never drift far off.
CS059.unlocked: XP made practices such as automated unit tests, continuous integration, refactoring and pair programming familiar across the industry. Its ideas went on to the agile movement, to Scrum-style iterations, and to today’s habits of continuous delivery and test-driven development, and its emphasis on customers and feedback changed how teams talk to the business. Unit-testing frameworks such as JUnit grew from this community. It showed that a development process could be defined by a few concrete, checkable habits.
CS059.left_open: XP works best for small teams with an engaged customer and code that can be tested; it is harder with large, distributed or safety-critical projects, and some practices, such as pair programming, divide opinion. Evidence for it came from experience and a few case studies, not controlled trials. Adopting a few practices without the rest can undo the benefits, and critics argued that it neglected up-front architecture. Beck himself revised the book in 2004, softening its stance.
CS059.diagram_alt: Six Extreme Programming practices arranged around a centre labelled short feedback loops: pair programming, tests first, small releases, refactoring, continuous integration and user stories.
review: Beck developed XP on Chrysler's C3 payroll project; first edition 1999, second edition 2004
JUnit grew from the XP and Smalltalk testing community (Beck and Gamma)
The 'cost of change curve' argument is Beck's framing
E111 (Brooks to XP) and E112 (XP to the Agile Manifesto) are interpretive

CS060.problem: By the end of the 1990s many software people were unhappy with heavyweight development methods, which promised control through detailed plans, documentation and sign-offs, but often delivered late, over budget and unwanted software. A number of alternative “lightweight” methods had appeared separately, each with its own name and following, among them Extreme Programming, Scrum, Crystal and Dynamic Systems Development. Their creators suspected they shared something, but there was no common statement and no common name for what they shared.
CS060.insight: In February 2001, seventeen practitioners met at a ski resort in Utah and wrote a short manifesto: four statements with a preamble. It says they value individuals and interactions over processes and tools; working software over comprehensive documentation; customer collaboration over contract negotiation; and responding to change over following a plan, adding that while there is value in the items on the right, they value the items on the left more. Twelve principles follow, such as delivering working software frequently, welcoming changing requirements even late in development, and keeping a sustainable pace. The group chose the word “agile” as the name for the shared approach, and the manifesto fits on a single page.
CS060.analogy: It is a statement of priorities, like a restaurant that says it values fresh food over a fancy menu. It does not forbid a menu, but when forced to choose, the food comes first.
CS060.unlocked: Agile became the mainstream way of developing software. Scrum, Kanban and XP are the best-known styles, and practices such as short iterations, daily meetings, backlogs and retrospectives are common even in organisations that would not call themselves agile. The manifesto reached beyond programming into management and product work, and underlies the culture of continuous delivery and DevOps. Its brevity helped it spread, and it gave a community of people a single word to rally around.
CS060.left_open: A manifesto states values, not methods, so “agile” has been stretched to cover very different practices, some of which its authors would not recognise; critics speak of cargo-cult agile and of rituals without the underlying spirit. Large organisations found it hard to scale, which produced frameworks that reintroduce heavy process. Evidence that it works better than other methods is mixed, and the manifesto says little about architecture, safety or hardware. Several signatories later criticised how it had been commercialised.
CS060.diagram_alt: The four value statements of the Agile Manifesto, each pairing what is valued more with what is valued less: individuals and interactions over processes and tools, working software over comprehensive documentation, customer collaboration over contract negotiation, responding to change over following a plan.
review: Seventeen signatories met at Snowbird, Utah, in February 2001
The four value statements are quoted in short form; the twelve principles are summarised
E099 (No Silver Bullet to Agile) and E112 (XP to Agile) are interpretive
Statements about later criticism by signatories are a common account, not claims from the manifesto

CS061.problem: Large web services run on many machines spread over networks that sometimes fail. Designers wanted three desirable properties: every request should see the latest data, as if there were a single copy, which is consistency; every request to a working machine should get a response, which is availability; and the system should keep working even when the network splits the machines into groups that cannot talk to each other, which is partition tolerance. In a 2000 keynote Eric Brewer conjectured that a system can have at most two of the three. It was an intuition, argued from experience, and not a precise statement.
CS061.insight: Seth Gilbert and Nancy Lynch made the conjecture precise and proved it. They fixed definitions: consistency means atomic, single-copy behaviour; availability means every request to a non-failed node eventually gets a response; and partitions mean messages between groups of nodes may be lost. The proof is short. Suppose a network splits in two, a write goes to one side, and a read goes to the other. The side that did not hear of the write must either answer, and possibly return stale data, losing consistency, or refuse to answer until it can talk to the other side, losing availability. Since a partition cannot be ruled out in a real network, the real choice is between consistency and availability during a partition. They also showed what is possible in weaker models, such as systems whose timing is partly synchronous.
CS061.analogy: Two bank branches lose their phone line. A customer asks one branch for the balance after a deposit made at the other. The clerk can either say what they last knew, which may be wrong, or say come back later. There is no third option.
CS061.unlocked: The CAP theorem became the common language for discussing trade-offs in distributed databases. It framed the design of Dynamo-style systems that favour availability and of systems that favour consistency, and it helped justify the rise of NoSQL stores and the idea of eventual consistency. Engineers use it to explain why a system behaves as it does in a failure. Brewer himself later clarified that the choice applies only during partitions, and that designers can choose per operation.
CS061.left_open: The theorem is narrow: it concerns a strong form of consistency and availability for every request, and real systems offer many levels in between, with latency also being a crucial trade-off the theorem ignores. “Pick two of three” became a misleading slogan: partitions are rare, so most of the time systems can offer both, and the theorem says nothing about what to do then. Later work, such as the PACELC formulation, tried to add what CAP leaves out.
CS061.diagram_alt: Two nodes whose network link is broken. A write goes to one node and a read to the other. The second node must either answer with possibly stale data, losing consistency, or refuse to answer, losing availability.
review: Brewer's conjecture was presented in his PODC 2000 keynote; Gilbert and Lynch's proof appeared in SIGACT News 2002
Brewer's later clarification: 'CAP twelve years later' (2012)
PACELC is due to Abadi
E113 (logical clocks to CAP) and E114 (CAP to Dynamo) are interpretive

CS062.problem: Google needed to store and process enormous amounts of data, crawled web pages, indexes and logs, measured in terabytes and soon petabytes, on clusters of thousands of cheap commodity machines. At that scale, disks and machines fail all the time, so failure had to be treated as normal, not exceptional. The workloads were also unusual: files of many gigabytes, written once, appended to by many programs and read in large sequential streams. Existing distributed file systems were designed for different assumptions, such as small files, random access and reliable hardware, and did not fit.
CS062.insight: The Google File System split the work between a single master and many chunkservers. Files are divided into large chunks of 64 megabytes, each stored on several chunkservers, by default three replicas. The master holds only the metadata, the namespace and where chunks are, in memory, and clients ask it where to go, then read and write data directly with the chunkservers, so the master is not a bottleneck. The master monitors chunkservers and recopies chunks when machines fail. The design relaxes the usual file-system guarantees: a special atomic append operation lets many clients add records to the same file concurrently, and the consistency model is deliberately loose, which applications tolerate in return for simplicity and speed.
CS062.analogy: Think of a library whose catalogue is kept by one librarian, while the books themselves are stored, in three copies each, across many warehouses. You ask the librarian where a book is, then go and fetch it yourself, and if a warehouse burns down, new copies are made from the others.
CS062.unlocked: GFS was the storage layer beneath Google’s search index and its other systems, including MapReduce and Bigtable, and it showed that reliable storage could be built from unreliable commodity parts. It inspired the open-source Hadoop Distributed File System, and with it much of the big-data ecosystem. The ideas of treating failure as routine, using large chunks, replicating, and having one coordinating master for metadata influenced many later storage systems.
CS062.left_open: A single master limits how large the system can grow and was a point of failure, which Google later addressed with a successor, Colossus, using distributed metadata. The 64-megabyte chunk is wasteful for small files, and the relaxed consistency requires applications to handle duplicates and inconsistencies. GFS was designed for Google’s own workloads, and suits latency-sensitive uses badly. The paper describes a working system but offers little theory of why its trade-offs are right.
CS062.diagram_alt: A client asks the master where a chunk is, then reads and writes data directly with chunkservers. Each chunk is stored on three of the chunkservers, so the loss of one machine leaves copies elsewhere.
review: Ghemawat, Gobioff and Leung, SOSP 2003; chunk size 64 MB and three replicas by default
Colossus is described as GFS's successor in later Google material
E115 (shared nothing to GFS) and E108 (PageRank search to GFS) are interpretive; E116 (GFS to MapReduce) and E117 (GFS to Bigtable) are tagged explicit

CS063.problem: Google’s engineers wrote many programs to process huge datasets, such as building indexes of crawled pages or counting how often words occur. Each program was conceptually simple, but running it on thousands of machines meant dealing with distributing the data, scheduling the work, handling machines that fail or run slowly, and collecting the results. This complicated code was rewritten again and again, and obscured the simple computation. Jeff Dean and Sanjay Ghemawat wanted a way for programmers without experience of distributed systems to use a big cluster.
CS063.insight: They proposed a programming model with just two functions that the user writes. The map function takes a piece of input and produces key-value pairs; the reduce function takes all the values that share a key and combines them. To count words, map emits each word with the number one, and reduce adds up the ones for each word. The system handles everything else: it splits the input among many machines, runs the map tasks near the data, shuffles the pairs so that all those with the same key come together, runs the reduce tasks, and writes the results. If a machine fails, its tasks are simply run again elsewhere, and slow ones are duplicated. The names come from the map and reduce functions of LISP and other functional languages.
CS063.analogy: Imagine counting votes across a country. Each polling station tallies its own ballots, a map step, and sends the tallies for each candidate to that candidate’s regional office, which adds them up, a reduce step. Nobody needs to see all the ballots.
CS063.unlocked: MapReduce made large-scale data processing accessible: thousands of Google programs were written in it within a few years. Its open-source counterpart, Hadoop, spread it across industry and started the big-data era. It established ideas that outlived it: that systems should handle failure automatically, that computation should move to the data, and that a restricted model can buy simplicity and scale. Its successors, such as Spark and Dataflow, relax its limits.
CS063.left_open: The model is restrictive: many tasks, such as iterative algorithms, graph processing and interactive queries, fit it poorly and are slow because every step reads and writes the disk. A few years later Google moved most of its work to other systems. Database researchers pointed out that it reinvented ideas from parallel databases without their query languages and optimisers. Tuning performance, and dealing with skew, where some keys have far more values, still takes expertise.
CS063.diagram_alt: A word-count example in four steps: input lines, map emitting word and one pairs, a shuffle grouping the pairs by word, and reduce adding up each group to give totals such as the 2, cat 2, dog 1 and sat 1.
review: Dean and Ghemawat, OSDI 2004; the paper says map and reduce were inspired by LISP and other functional languages (basis for E118, tagged explicit)
Hadoop is the open-source implementation; Spark and Dataflow are later systems
E096, E124 are interpretive; E116 (GFS to MapReduce) is tagged explicit

CS064.problem: Google’s products, such as web search, Google Earth and Gmail, needed to store huge amounts of structured data, billions of rows and petabytes, with very different demands: some wanted high throughput for batch processing, others low latency for serving users. Traditional relational databases could not be scaled to this size at reasonable cost, or would have needed expensive, specialised designs. Files in GFS were too raw for these applications, which wanted something like a database table, but one built for scale.
CS064.insight: Bigtable is a distributed storage system that presents a simple data model: a sparse, sorted, multidimensional map. Data is addressed by a row key, a column name and a timestamp, so a table can hold many versions of each cell. Rows are kept in sorted order and split into ranges called tablets, each served by one machine, and tablets move between machines for balance and recovery. Columns are grouped into families. Underneath, data is written to immutable sorted files, called SSTables, in the Google File System, with recent writes held in memory and in a log and merged in the background; a distributed lock service, Chubby, elects the master and tracks servers. It deliberately offers no joins and only single-row transactions.
CS064.analogy: It is like a giant ledger whose rows are kept in alphabetical order and torn into volumes, each kept by one clerk. To find a row you find the volume, and every cell remembers its earlier versions by date.
CS064.unlocked: Bigtable demonstrated that a scalable table store could serve both batch and real-time workloads, and it powered dozens of Google products. Its design inspired a family of wide-column stores, including HBase and Cassandra, and much of the NoSQL movement, and the log-structured merge approach it used became common in modern storage engines. Together with GFS and MapReduce, it formed the template of Google’s infrastructure that the open-source world then copied.
CS064.left_open: By giving up joins, secondary indexes and multi-row transactions, Bigtable pushed complexity to applications, which had to build their own, and Google later built Megastore and Spanner to restore transactions and stronger consistency. Its reliance on a single master per cluster and on Chubby are points of dependency. Tuning it requires care with row keys and hot spots. And the paper reports experience and performance but, like other systems papers, offers few guarantees.
CS064.diagram_alt: A table whose rows are sorted by key, with column families, and cells that hold several timestamped versions. Ranges of rows form tablets, each served by one machine.
review: Chang et al., OSDI 2006; data model: row key, column family:qualifier, timestamp
The table in the diagram is a schematic example in the paper's webtable style
E117 (GFS to Bigtable) and E119 (Bigtable to Spanner) are tagged explicit; verify the Spanner paper's statement about Bigtable-like tablets

CS065.problem: Organisations hold data about people, such as medical records, search queries and census answers, and want to share statistics from it. Removing names does not protect privacy: researchers repeatedly re-identified supposedly anonymous records by linking them with other data. Simple remedies such as suppressing small counts failed too, since a few queries can be combined to reveal an individual. And earlier definitions asked that an outsider learn nothing about anyone, which Dwork showed is impossible if the outsider has any outside knowledge. A precise, achievable definition of privacy was missing.
CS065.insight: Cynthia Dwork proposed differential privacy. A randomised computation is differentially private if its output is almost equally likely whether or not any one person’s data is included. Formally, changing a single person’s record changes the probability of any output by at most a factor of e raised to ε, a small number the designer chooses. Then whatever an attacker knows, and whatever else they can learn from the result, the answer reveals almost nothing about whether you took part, so taking part cannot harm you much. The way to achieve it is to add carefully calibrated random noise to the answer, scaled to how much one person could change it, the sensitivity. The parameter ε sets a privacy budget, which is spent as more queries are answered, and the guarantees compose.
CS065.analogy: It is like a survey in which each answer is slightly blurred by a coin flip. The overall rate stays accurate for a big crowd, yet nobody can be sure of any one person’s true answer, because any single answer might have come from the coin.
CS065.unlocked: Differential privacy gave the field a rigorous, composable definition, and it became the leading framework for privacy-preserving data analysis. It has been used for the US Census Bureau’s 2020 release, and by companies including Apple, Google and Microsoft to gather usage statistics, and it is used in tools for training machine-learning models without leaking their training data. It created a research field that links computer science, statistics, law and ethics.
CS065.left_open: Privacy is bought with accuracy. Strong guarantees add enough noise to harm small datasets and detailed statistics, and choosing ε is a social decision with no agreed answer. The budget limits how many questions can be asked. Guarantees apply to what the mechanism releases, and are weakened when data about the same person appears in many records, or when others can infer things from correlated data. Deploying it correctly is subtle, and implementation errors can destroy the guarantee.
CS065.diagram_alt: Two almost overlapping probability curves: the distribution of a noisy answer computed with one person's data included and without it. The probabilities differ by at most a factor of e to the epsilon, so the answer reveals almost nothing about any individual.
review: Dwork, ICALP 2006; related paper by Dwork, McSherry, Nissim and Smith, 'Calibrating noise to sensitivity' (2006)
The 2020 US Census used differential privacy; the company deployments named are from public announcements
E123 (Shannon to differential privacy) is an interpretive reading

CS066.problem: Amazon’s online store ran on thousands of servers, and for some services, such as the shopping cart, being unavailable even briefly meant lost sales and lost customer trust. Failures of disks, servers and networks were constant, and a data centre could go offline. The relational databases in use did not scale well, and offered strong consistency at the price of availability when something failed. The cart did not need complex queries: it needed to always accept a write, and to hold a simple item looked up by key.
CS066.insight: Dynamo is a key-value store designed to be always writeable. It spreads data around a ring using consistent hashing, so machines can be added or removed with only small parts of the data moving, and replicates each item on several successive nodes. Reads and writes go to a configurable number of replicas, with the settings N, R and W letting an application trade consistency for speed and availability. When a replica is unreachable, another node temporarily takes its writes, called hinted handoff, and gives them back later. Updates can conflict, so Dynamo does not force a single order: it records versions with vector clocks and lets the application, or the system, reconcile conflicts when they are read. Nodes find each other and detect failure with gossip, and there is no master.
CS066.analogy: Think of a shop with many tills that always take your order even if the line between them is down, writing it on a slip. When the line comes back, the slips are compared and any clashes sorted out. A customer is never turned away.
CS066.unlocked: Dynamo made the case for eventual consistency in production and shaped the NoSQL movement: its design was the model for Cassandra, Riak and Voldemort, and it led to Amazon’s DynamoDB service. Techniques it popularised, consistent hashing, sloppy quorums, vector clocks for versioning, gossip protocols and anti-entropy with Merkle trees, became a standard toolkit for building distributed databases.
CS066.left_open: Pushing conflict resolution onto applications makes them harder to write, and some developers prefer stronger guarantees. Dynamo gave up on rich queries and on strong consistency for the sake of availability. Eventually consistent reads can return stale data, which is unacceptable for some uses, such as financial transactions. Amazon itself later built services with stronger consistency. And the paper’s system was tuned for Amazon’s workload and trust within one organisation, not for the open internet.
CS066.diagram_alt: A ring of six nodes. A key is hashed to a position on the ring and stored on that node and the next two, three replicas in all. Notes describe N, R and W settings that trade consistency for speed and availability, and vector clocks for conflicting versions.
review: DeCandia et al., SOSP 2007; Dynamo is an internal system; DynamoDB is a later managed service with a different design
Techniques named: consistent hashing, sloppy quorum and hinted handoff, vector clocks, gossip, Merkle-tree anti-entropy
E114, E120, E121 and E125 are interpretive

CS067.problem: Online payments depended on trusted third parties, banks and payment companies, to prevent the central problem of digital money: double-spending. A digital coin is just data, and data can be copied, so someone must keep a record of who has spent what. A trusted intermediary can do this, but it adds costs, can refuse or reverse transactions, and must be trusted by everyone. Earlier attempts at digital cash had foundered on the need for a central authority. Could a payment system exist with no such authority, among strangers who do not trust one another?
CS067.insight: The paper, by the pseudonymous Satoshi Nakamoto, proposes a peer-to-peer network that keeps a public ledger of all transactions. Transactions are signed with public-key cryptography, so only the owner of a coin can spend it. They are gathered into blocks, and each block contains the hash of the previous one, forming a chain. To add a block, a participant must solve a puzzle that takes much computing work, proof of work, a technique borrowed from Hashcash, by finding a number that makes the block’s hash small. The network accepts the longest chain as the truth, and the one who adds a block earns new coins, which is the incentive. To rewrite history, an attacker would have to redo the work of every later block and outpace all the honest participants, which is impractical unless they control most of the computing power.
CS067.analogy: Imagine a public notebook that everyone copies, in which each page is sealed with a wax stamp that takes enormous effort to make and also covers the page before it. Altering an old page would mean re-stamping every page after it, faster than the rest of the town can add new ones.
CS067.unlocked: Bitcoin launched in January 2009 and became the first working decentralised digital currency. It showed that a ledger could be kept by strangers without a trusted party, and it started the field of blockchains and cryptocurrencies, with thousands of followers, smart contracts and decentralised finance. It revived interest in distributed consensus, in the Byzantine generals’ problem in open networks, and in applied cryptography and game theory.
CS067.left_open: Proof of work uses a great deal of electricity, and it limits throughput to a handful of transactions per second. Security depends on an honest majority of computing power, which can concentrate, and on assumptions about incentives. Transactions are public and, despite pseudonyms, can often be traced. Irreversibility is harmful when mistakes or thefts occur, and the technology attracted fraud and speculation. Whether it works as everyday money, as opposed to as a speculative asset, is still contested.
CS067.diagram_alt: A chain of blocks, each holding transactions, a proof-of-work number and the hash of the previous block. Rewriting an old block would mean redoing the work for every block after it, so the longest chain is the one accepted as true.
review: Nakamoto's paper cites Hashcash (Back), Merkle trees and Haber and Stornetta's timestamping (basis for ghost G016 and edge E122, tagged explicit)
The network launched in January 2009
E077 (public-key cryptography) and E089 (Byzantine generals) are interpretive

CS068.problem: By 2011, computer vision had made steady but slow progress. The best systems for recognising objects in photographs first computed hand-designed features, such as edges and gradients, and then fed them to a classifier like a support-vector machine. The annual ImageNet challenge, built from more than a million labelled photographs in a thousand categories, measured progress, and the winning error rate improved only in small steps. Neural networks that learn their own features were an old idea, but they were widely believed to be too slow to train on a dataset of that size, and too prone to overfitting.
CS068.insight: Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton trained a large convolutional neural network, with eight learned layers and about sixty million parameters, on the ImageNet photographs. Convolutional layers apply small filters that scan across the image, so that the same detector is reused everywhere, which fits the structure of pictures. To make training feasible they ran it on two graphics processors, GPUs, which are very fast at the kind of arithmetic involved, and used several tricks: the ReLU activation, which trains faster than older smooth functions; dropout, which randomly switches off neurons during training so that the network cannot rely on any one of them; and data augmentation, which makes extra training examples by cropping and flipping the images. Features were no longer designed by hand but learned from the data.
CS068.analogy: Instead of teaching a child to recognise animals by handing over a checklist of features, such as pointy ears and whiskers, you let them look at a million photographs and work out for themselves which patterns matter.
CS068.unlocked: AlexNet won the 2012 ImageNet competition with a top-five error of about 15 per cent, when the runner-up had about 26, a gap that startled the field. Within a couple of years nearly every vision system used deep convolutional networks, and the approach spread to speech, translation, games and science. It set off the deep-learning boom, drew industry into AI research, and made GPUs the standard hardware for machine learning. Hinton, with Bengio and LeCun, received the Turing Award in 2018.
CS068.left_open: The result depended on a huge labelled dataset and costly computing, which only some labs could afford. Networks were hard to understand and could be fooled by tiny changes to an image, and they learned whatever patterns were in the data, including its biases. Going deeper than eight layers proved difficult, which the next advances addressed. And recognising an object in a photograph is far from understanding a scene.
CS068.diagram_alt: A schematic of AlexNet: a photograph passes through five convolutional layers that learn filters and three fully connected layers to a thousand-way answer. Two bars compare the 2012 ImageNet top-five error of 15.3 per cent for AlexNet against 26.2 per cent for the runner-up.
review: Krizhevsky, Sutskever and Hinton, NIPS 2012; 8 learned layers (5 convolutional, 3 fully connected), about 60 million parameters, two GPUs
Top-5 error 15.3% versus 26.2% for the runner-up in the 2012 ImageNet challenge
Turing Award 2018 (Hinton, Bengio, LeCun)
E126 (LeNet to AlexNet) is tagged explicit: the paper builds on LeCun's convolutional networks; verify
E095 (backpropagation) and E127 (SVMs overtaken) are interpretive

CS069.problem: Google ran services such as advertising and Gmail on data spread over many datacentres around the world, and engineers faced an uncomfortable choice. Systems like Bigtable scaled well and survived datacentre failures, but offered only weak guarantees: no transactions across rows, and replicas that might disagree. Traditional relational databases offered transactions and strong consistency, but could not spread over the globe or scale to Google’s size. Applications that needed both, such as the advertising database, had been kept on a manually divided collection of MySQL servers that was painful to maintain.
CS069.insight: Spanner is a globally distributed database that offers strong consistency, so that transactions appear to run one after another in a single order, even across continents. It divides data into shards, replicates each shard across datacentres with Paxos, and runs distributed transactions across shards with two-phase commit. The key innovation is TrueTime, a clock interface that does not claim to know the exact time but returns an interval within which the true time must lie, kept narrow, a few milliseconds, by GPS receivers and atomic clocks in every datacentre. Spanner gives each transaction a commit timestamp and, before making it visible, waits until the uncertainty has passed, so that timestamps agree with real time. This gives external consistency and lets read-only transactions and reads of past snapshots run without locks.
CS069.analogy: Imagine a worldwide chain of banks that stamps every transaction with the time. If each branch knows its clock might be off by a few milliseconds, it simply waits that long before announcing a deposit, so that no other branch can later stamp an earlier event with a later time.
CS069.unlocked: Spanner showed that the supposed trade-off between scale and strong consistency could be pushed much further than the CAP theorem’s slogan suggested, by controlling the network and the clocks. It brought SQL, schemas and transactions back to a planet-scale database, and inspired a family of “NewSQL” systems such as CockroachDB and YugabyteDB, as well as Google’s own Cloud Spanner service. TrueTime made the case that precise clocks are a building block of distributed systems.
CS069.left_open: Spanner depends on infrastructure few can copy: GPS and atomic clocks in every datacentre, and Google’s private network. Commit latency includes the wait for clock uncertainty and the cost of cross-datacentre replication, so writes across continents are slow. Distributed transactions are costly under contention. And the paper describes the system as it stood: schema changes, query optimisation and performance continued to evolve, and others have built imitations without the special clock hardware.
CS069.diagram_alt: A shard replicated across three datacentres by Paxos. Below, a timeline of TrueTime: the clock returns an interval of earliest and latest possible times, and a transaction picks a commit timestamp and waits until that timestamp is certainly in the past before becoming visible.
review: Corbett et al., OSDI 2012; TrueTime uses GPS and atomic clocks, with uncertainty of a few milliseconds
Spanner uses Paxos for replication (basis for E110, tagged explicit) and Bigtable-like tablets (E119, tagged explicit); verify both against the paper
CockroachDB and YugabyteDB are Spanner-inspired; Cloud Spanner is Google's service
E084, E121 and E130 are interpretive

CS070.problem: Generative models learn to produce new data that looks like their training data, such as new images, rather than just to classify it. The existing approaches had awkward drawbacks. Some needed to calculate probabilities that were intractable for complex data, others required long and approximate sampling procedures, and the images they made, especially of faces, were blurry. Ian Goodfellow and his colleagues wanted a generative model that avoided these difficulties and could use the full power of neural networks trained by backpropagation.
CS070.insight: The idea of generative adversarial networks is to train two networks against each other. A generator takes random noise and tries to produce a convincing fake, such as an image. A discriminator is shown a mixture of real examples and the generator’s fakes, and tries to tell them apart. They are trained together as a game: the discriminator is rewarded for spotting fakes, the generator for fooling it. As each improves, the other must improve. In the ideal limit the generator reproduces the data so well that the discriminator can do no better than guess. Neither network needs an explicit formula for the probability of the data; both are trained with ordinary backpropagation. The paper shows the game has an ideal solution, and demonstrates it on handwritten digits, faces and small photographs.
CS070.analogy: A forger and an art detective. The forger paints copies; the detective examines paintings and says which are fake. Each round, the forger learns from what gave the work away, and the detective learns to spot subtler flaws, until the forgeries are indistinguishable.
CS070.unlocked: GANs produced some of the first strikingly realistic synthetic images, and a flood of variants followed, for generating faces, translating photographs between styles, increasing resolution and creating art. They helped make “generative AI” a research field, and raised public concern about deepfakes. The adversarial idea, training one model against another, spread to many other problems, including improving robustness and learning from unlabelled data. Diffusion models later took over much of the image-generation work.
CS070.left_open: GANs are notoriously hard to train: the two networks can fall out of balance, the generator can collapse to producing a few repetitive outputs, and training can fail to settle. Evaluating them is difficult, since no single number says how good the samples are. They do not give the probability of a sample, and they can miss parts of the data. For text and other discrete data they work poorly, and diffusion models and large language models mostly displaced them.
CS070.diagram_alt: Random noise enters a generator that produces fake images. Real images and fakes both go to a discriminator that says real or fake. Dashed arrows show each network learning from the discriminator's verdict, so the generator improves at fooling it.
review: Goodfellow et al., NIPS 2014; the minimax game and its ideal solution are in the paper
Both networks are trained by backpropagation (basis for E129, tagged explicit)
Diffusion models later displaced GANs for much image generation: a common account, not the paper's claim

CS071.problem: Consensus, getting several machines to agree on a sequence of values even when some fail, is at the heart of reliable distributed systems. Paxos, the standard solution since 1998, was proven correct, but Diego Ongaro and John Ousterhout, at Stanford, found it very hard to understand and teach, even for graduate students and experienced engineers. Worse, the basic Paxos algorithm decides a single value, so every real system had to extend it to a full replicated log in its own way, and the resulting systems often differed from the published algorithm and were poorly specified. They set out to design a consensus algorithm whose main goal was understandability.
CS071.insight: Raft breaks the problem into three relatively independent parts. In leader election, one server is elected leader for a numbered term, using randomised timeouts to avoid ties. In log replication, the leader accepts client commands, appends them to its log and copies them to the other servers; an entry is committed once a majority has stored it, and the leader tells the others. Safety rules ensure that a server can win an election only if its log contains all committed entries, so a committed command is never lost, and that followers’ logs are made to match the leader’s. Membership changes are handled by a joint-consensus step. By decomposing the problem and reducing the number of states to consider, the authors made the algorithm simpler to reason about, and they backed that up with a user study in which students found Raft easier to learn than Paxos.
CS071.analogy: Think of a classroom with one teacher at a time. If the teacher leaves, the students elect a new one, and only someone who already has all the notes can win. Everyone copies down what the teacher writes, and a note counts once most of the class has it.
CS071.unlocked: Raft quickly became the default choice for consensus in new systems. It is used in etcd, which holds Kubernetes’ cluster state, in Consul, in CockroachDB and many other databases, and has implementations in dozens of languages. It made fault-tolerant replication approachable to engineers who would not have built it with Paxos. And it showed that understandability can be a design goal for algorithms, worth testing with users.
CS071.left_open: Raft solves the same crash-fault problem as Paxos, with the same limits: it does not tolerate malicious servers, and a single leader can become a bottleneck, since all writes pass through it. Whether Raft really is simpler in depth is debated, and the study’s evidence is limited to one group of students. Real systems still need many extras beyond the paper, such as log compaction, snapshotting and careful handling of reads. And performance trade-offs differ from leaderless variants.
CS071.diagram_alt: Three servers' logs of numbered entries labelled with their term. The leader and one follower hold five entries and the third follower holds four. Entries held by a majority are committed. Three parts are named: elect a leader, replicate the log, and stay safe.
review: Ongaro and Ousterhout, USENIX ATC 2014; user study with students comparing Raft and Paxos

CS072.problem: After AlexNet, results improved as networks got deeper: more layers can learn more complex patterns, and the winners of the ImageNet contests grew from 8 to around 20 layers. But Kaiming He and colleagues at Microsoft Research noticed a puzzling problem. When they made a plain network deeper still, its accuracy got worse, even on the training data. This was not overfitting; the deeper network had the capacity to do at least as well, since it could in principle copy a shallower one and make its extra layers do nothing, but the training procedure could not find that solution. They called it the degradation problem.
CS072.insight: Their remedy is to change what each block of layers must learn. Instead of asking a few layers to learn the desired mapping from scratch, they add a shortcut that carries the block’s input straight to its output, and the layers learn only the residual, the difference between the output and the input. If the best thing for a block is to do nothing, it only has to set the residual to zero, which is easy, and the identity connections also let the training signal flow directly through very many layers. With this one change, they trained networks of 50, 101 and 152 layers, and even a 1,000-layer one on a small dataset, and the deeper they were, the better they did, winning the 2015 ImageNet competition with a 3.6 per cent top-five error, below the estimated human rate of about 5 per cent.
CS072.analogy: Instead of rewriting a whole essay in each round of editing, an editor marks only the corrections. If a page is already fine, the corrections are nothing, and the page passes through untouched.
CS072.unlocked: Residual connections let networks go from tens of layers to hundreds and beyond, and became a standard ingredient of almost every modern deep network. They are in the Transformers that power language models, in image models and in scientific ones such as AlphaFold. ResNet itself became the default backbone for computer vision. The paper is among the most cited in all of science.
CS072.left_open: The paper shows that residual networks train better, but explanations of why remain partly informal: whether it is the smoother loss landscape, the shorter effective paths, or something else is still discussed. Very deep networks are costly to run, and later work found that wide and efficient networks can do as well with fewer layers. And better accuracy on benchmarks like ImageNet does not by itself ensure robustness, fairness or understanding.
CS072.diagram_alt: A residual block: the input x goes through two layers that compute F of x, while a shortcut carries x unchanged around them. The two are added to give F of x plus x. A note says the layers learn the change, not the whole mapping, which allowed networks of 152 layers and more.

CS073.problem: Google ran hundreds of thousands of jobs, from many thousands of different applications, across clusters of tens of thousands of machines. Some were user-facing services that must always be up, such as Gmail or search; others were batch jobs such as MapReduce that run for a while and finish. Placing them by hand on particular machines was impossible, machines failed all the time, and keeping the machines busy mattered, since each idle machine was money wasted. Google needed a system that would take a description of what to run and make it happen reliably, and efficiently, across the whole cluster.
CS073.insight: Borg is Google’s cluster manager. Users submit jobs, made of many identical tasks, with a statement of the resources each needs, and Borg decides where to run them. A logically centralised controller, the Borgmaster, replicated five times with its state in a Paxos-based store, tracks all machines and tasks, while a Borglet agent on each machine starts and monitors tasks. A scheduler scores candidate machines to pack tasks tightly and spread risk. Several ideas make it efficient: jobs have priorities, so batch work can fill gaps and be preempted when a service needs room; resources are over-committed on the bet that not all tasks use their full request at once; and tasks run in containers on shared machines. Borg restarts failed tasks automatically and provides naming and monitoring.
CS073.analogy: Think of a port that packs containers into ships. Instead of each company choosing a ship, a central planner fits cargo into the available space, loads urgent goods first, and reloads quickly if a ship is delayed or lost.
CS073.unlocked: Borg made it possible to run vast numbers of services efficiently and reliably, and engineers could deploy without thinking about individual machines at all. Its lessons became Kubernetes, the open-source container orchestrator that Google released in 2014, now the standard way to run cloud applications, and shaped ideas such as containers, microservices and declarative configuration. The paper, written a decade after Borg’s start, also set out what the authors learned, which helped the industry.
CS073.left_open: Borg’s job model and its many configuration options became hard to manage, and the design had accumulated complexity; the authors list things they would do differently, such as making jobs less rigid and providing better tools for users. Scheduling decisions at this scale are heuristic and hard to predict, and sharing machines causes interference between tasks. The paper describes a system tied to Google’s particular workloads and tooling, so its lessons may carry less to smaller organisations.
CS073.diagram_alt: A Borgmaster, replicated five times, schedules tasks onto four machines. Each machine runs user-facing service tasks in blue and batch tasks in orange side by side, with priorities deciding which waits. Failed tasks are restarted automatically.

CS074.problem: In many companies, the people who build software and the people who run it are separate teams with opposing goals. Developers want to ship new features quickly; operations staff, who are woken when things break, want stability. The result is friction, slow releases and a lot of manual work by operations teams that grows with the size of the service. Google, running some of the largest services ever built, could not afford that model: hiring more operators in step with growth was impossible, and the old division of labour made both speed and reliability suffer.
CS074.insight: Site Reliability Engineering, described in the book by Betsy Beyer and colleagues, applies a software engineering approach to operating systems. SREs are engineers who write code to automate operations, and the book sets a limit: no more than half their time on routine “toil,” the rest on engineering that removes it. Reliability is treated as a feature with a measurable target, a service level objective, such as 99.9 per cent of requests succeeding. The gap between that target and perfection is an error budget: while there is budget left, developers may release quickly; when it is spent, releases slow until reliability recovers. This turns the argument between speed and stability into a shared number. Other practices include blameless postmortems after failures, careful monitoring built on a few key signals, and handing back services that are too unreliable to support.
CS074.analogy: Think of a household budget. If you set aside a fixed amount to spend on treats, you can spend freely until it is gone, without arguing every time, and when it runs out, everyone knows it is time to stop.
CS074.unlocked: The book made SRE a recognised profession and spread its vocabulary, service level objectives, error budgets, toil and blameless postmortems, across the industry, where it shaped DevOps practice and the operation of cloud services. It gave organisations a way to reconcile development speed with reliability, and a framework for deciding how reliable a service needs to be. Companies adopted its roles, and its follow-ups, a workbook and a book on building secure and reliable systems, extended it.
CS074.left_open: The model comes from Google’s scale, and many of its practices, such as large dedicated SRE teams, do not carry over to smaller companies, which have adapted it with mixed results. Error budgets and targets need agreement and honest measurement, and can be gamed. The book is a collection of essays by many authors, with differing styles, not a rigorous study, and its claims rest on experience. Burnout and on-call load remain real concerns.
CS074.diagram_alt: An error budget as a gauge: the reliability target of 99.9 per cent leaves a small budget for failures. While budget remains, developers release freely; when it is spent, releases slow until reliability recovers. A note says engineers spend at most half their time on toil.
review: Beyer, Jones, Petoff and Murphy (eds.), O'Reilly 2016; follow-ups: the SRE Workbook (2018) and Building Secure and Reliable Systems (2020)

CS075.problem: By 2016 the best models for language, translation, summarisation and speech were recurrent neural networks, such as LSTMs, which read a sentence one word at a time, carrying a summary of what they have seen. This sequential design has two drawbacks. It cannot be parallelised across the words of a sentence, since each step waits for the previous one, so training is slow on modern hardware. And information from far apart words must pass through many steps to meet, so long-range relationships are hard to learn. Attention, a mechanism that lets a model look back at any part of the input when producing each output word, had been added to recurrent networks and helped a great deal.
CS075.insight: Ashish Vaswani and colleagues at Google asked whether attention alone would be enough, with no recurrence at all. The Transformer processes all the words of a sequence at once. In each layer, self-attention lets every word compute a weighted combination of all the others: each word makes a query, and compares it with the keys of every word to decide how much of each word’s value to take in. Several attention “heads” work in parallel to capture different kinds of relationship, and position information is added to the word vectors since order is otherwise lost. Layers also contain feed-forward networks and residual connections. Because everything is done with large matrix multiplications, it trains much faster on GPUs, and any two words are connected in a single step. On English-to-German and English-to-French translation it set new records at a fraction of the training cost.
CS075.analogy: Reading a sentence in a meeting where everyone can address everyone else at once: each person decides whose comments matter for their own, and listens most to those, instead of passing a message down a line one person at a time.
CS075.unlocked: The Transformer became the foundation of modern AI. BERT, GPT and their successors, the large language models behind chat assistants, are Transformers, and the architecture spread to vision, speech, protein structure, music and robotics. Its parallelism made it practical to train on vast datasets, which let performance keep improving as models and data grew, a trend that now drives the field. The paper is among the most cited in computer science.
CS075.left_open: Self-attention compares every word with every other, so cost grows with the square of the sequence length, which limits how much text a model can read at once and has driven a lot of work on cheaper variants. Transformers need huge amounts of data and computing, and are hard to interpret; what they actually learn remains debated. They are sometimes unreliable in reasoning and in making things up.
CS075.diagram_alt: The sentence the cat sat on the mat with arcs of different thickness from the word sat to every other word, showing that each word attends to all the others at once. Below, the building blocks of a layer: self-attention, a feed-forward network, residual connections and added position information.

CS076.problem: To teach a computer a language task, such as answering questions or judging whether two sentences agree, you used to need a lot of labelled examples for that specific task, and the model started from nothing. Pretraining on plain text, which requires no labels, had begun to help: models learned word meanings from large amounts of text and were then adapted. But the leading approaches read text in one direction, left to right, or combined two one-directional models only shallowly, so each word’s representation could use only the context on one side at a time, a limit for tasks that depend on understanding a whole sentence.
CS076.insight: Jacob Devlin and colleagues at Google built BERT, Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers, on the encoder of the Transformer. To let every word use context from both sides without cheating, they pretrained it with a fill-in-the-blank game, masked language modelling: about 15 per cent of the words in a sentence are hidden, and the model must predict them from the rest. A second task, predicting whether one sentence follows another, helped with tasks involving sentence pairs. Pretraining on a large amount of unlabelled text, Wikipedia and a corpus of books, gives a general model that can then be fine-tuned for a task by adding a small output layer and training briefly on a small labelled dataset. BERT set new records on eleven language-understanding tasks.
CS076.analogy: It is like learning a language by doing endless fill-in-the-blank exercises on millions of pages. Having done that, you can quickly pick up almost any particular task, such as answering questions or sorting reviews, with only a few examples.
CS076.unlocked: BERT made pretrain-then-fine-tune the standard recipe for language tasks, and quickly transformed natural language processing: Google added it to its search in 2019, and it spawned many variants, such as RoBERTa, DistilBERT and domain-specific models, and open checkpoints that anyone could download and adapt. It brought strong language understanding within reach of small teams, since the expensive pretraining was done once and shared.
CS076.left_open: BERT reads but does not write: its design suits classification and extraction, not generating text, and the next wave of models, GPT and others, took the generative path. It needs fine-tuning with labelled data for each task, a step later models tried to avoid. It is expensive to pretrain, and the masked words are unlike real use, in which no words are hidden. And it inherits the biases of its training text, which are hard to detect and correct.
CS076.diagram_alt: The sentence the mask sat on the mask goes into a Transformer encoder that looks at words on both sides, and predicts the hidden words cat and mat. Below, two steps: pretrain on a large amount of unlabelled text, then fine-tune on a small labelled set.

CS077.problem: Pretrained language models like BERT could be adapted to many tasks, but each adaptation still needed its own collection of labelled examples, often thousands, and fine-tuning produced a separate specialised model for every task. Humans do not work like this: we can do a new language task from a brief instruction, or from a handful of examples. The OpenAI team asked whether making a language model much larger would let it pick up new tasks the way people do, from a few examples, with no further training at all.
CS077.insight: GPT-3 is a Transformer decoder trained on a simple objective: predict the next word of a text. It has 175 billion parameters, ten times more than any earlier dense model, and was trained on hundreds of billions of words from the Internet, books and Wikipedia. The paper’s central finding is in-context learning. Without changing any weights, you describe a task in the prompt, perhaps giving a few examples, and the model continues the pattern: translate, answer questions, correct grammar, do arithmetic, write stories or code. Performance on many tasks improved smoothly with model size, and the few-shot setting, giving a handful of examples, often matched fine-tuned models. The authors tested it on dozens of benchmarks, and noted its limits and risks.
CS077.analogy: Instead of retraining an employee for each new job, you hand them a note: “here are three examples of what I want, now do the fourth.” A well-read assistant can often work out what is wanted from the examples alone.
CS077.unlocked: GPT-3 showed that scale could unlock general abilities that nobody had programmed, and it made prompting the main way of using a model. It led to ChatGPT, through further training on instructions and human feedback, and to a wave of commercial products and open models, from writing assistants to programming tools such as Codex and Copilot. The scaling-laws view of progress, that more data, parameters and computing keep improving results, became the strategy of the field.
CS077.left_open: GPT-3 makes things up fluently, can be confidently wrong, and has no reliable way to say when it does not know. It reflects biases, toxicity and errors in its training text, a risk the paper itself discusses. Training such models costs millions of dollars and a great deal of energy, so only a few organisations can do it, and the model was released only as a paid service. Why in-context learning works, and how far it can go, is still being studied. And a model that predicts words is not the same as one that understands or reasons.
CS077.diagram_alt: A prompt that gives two English to French examples, sea otter to loutre de mer and cheese to fromage, and then asks for bread. A model with 175 billion parameters, trained only to predict the next word, continues the pattern with pain, with no further training.

CS078.problem: Large language models like GPT-3 had shown some ability to write code, as the Internet is full of it, but they were not good at it, and nobody had a good way to measure how good they were. Standard text-matching measures such as BLEU, borrowed from translation, are a poor test of programs: two programs can be written very differently and both be correct, or look almost identical and one be wrong. If a model was to be a useful programming assistant, it needed training on code in earnest, and a test of whether the code it writes actually works.
CS078.insight: OpenAI researchers fine-tuned GPT models on a large body of public code from GitHub, creating Codex. To evaluate it, they built HumanEval, a set of 164 handwritten programming problems, each with a function signature, a description and unit tests. The measure is functional correctness: the model writes a function, and it counts only if it passes the tests. They report pass@k, the chance that at least one of k generated samples passes. The largest Codex model solved about 29 per cent of the problems on the first try, and about 72 per cent when allowed 100 attempts, whereas GPT-3 solved almost none. Sampling many candidates and picking the best, for instance by running tests, helped greatly. The paper also discusses limits, safety, security and economic impacts.
CS078.analogy: Judging a student’s programming exam by whether the answer contains the right words is a poor test. A better test is to run the student’s code against a set of checks and see whether it passes.
CS078.unlocked: Codex powered GitHub Copilot, launched in 2021, which brought AI code completion to millions of developers, and it began the wave of coding assistants and code models. HumanEval and pass@k became standard ways to compare code models, and the idea of testing generated code by running it, rather than reading it, shaped later benchmarks and training methods. The paper set the template for treating programming as a domain for language models.
CS078.left_open: HumanEval is small and made of short, self-contained functions, far from real software engineering; models can have seen similar problems in their training data, which is difficult to rule out. Generated code can be subtly wrong, insecure or insufficiently tested, and developers may trust it too much. The paper notes concerns about licensing of the code trained on, and about misuse and labour effects. And passing the tests is only part of writing good software: design, maintainability and fitting an existing codebase are not measured.
CS078.diagram_alt: A function signature and description are given to the model, which writes the body. Unit tests then run on the generated code and it counts only if they pass. The largest model solved about 29 per cent of problems at one attempt and about 72 per cent at a hundred attempts.
review: Chen et al. (OpenAI), arXiv 2021; Codex is GPT fine-tuned on public GitHub code; HumanEval has 164 problems; pass@k
The largest Codex model: about 28.8% at pass@1 and about 72.3% at pass@100 (as reported); GPT-3 solved essentially none

CS079.problem: By 2023, language models were passing the short function-writing tests such as HumanEval with ease, but real software work is not like that. Professional engineers read a large codebase, find where a bug lies or where a feature belongs, change several files, and make sure existing tests still pass. A model that writes a clean ten-line function from a description may still be unable to do any of this. The existing benchmarks no longer separated the stronger models, and there was no measure of whether a model could do the work of fixing real issues.
CS079.insight: Carlos Jimenez and colleagues built SWE-bench from real work: 2,294 issues, bug reports and feature requests, from twelve popular Python open-source projects such as Django, scikit-learn and sympy, each paired with the pull request that the human developers wrote to resolve it. A model is given the repository and the text of the issue, and must produce a patch. The patch is checked by running the project’s tests: tests that the human fix made pass must now pass, and tests that passed before must still pass. This tests the whole skill: understanding a large codebase, locating the problem, editing across files and respecting existing behaviour. The authors found that, at the time, the best models resolved only a few per cent of issues; the strongest, Claude 2, solved under 2 per cent.
CS079.analogy: It is the difference between a driving test on an empty car park and one on real streets in traffic. Passing the first says little about the second.
CS079.unlocked: SWE-bench became the leading benchmark for AI software engineering. Progress on it was rapid: later systems built around language models, with tools for browsing and running code, resolved a much larger share of the problems, and companies compete on its leaderboard. It shaped the design of coding agents, which edit files, run tests and iterate, and a human-checked subset, SWE-bench Verified, was released to improve reliability. It moved the question from whether a model can write code to whether it can do an engineer’s job.
CS079.left_open: SWE-bench covers a limited set of Python repositories and issues with good tests, and does not capture design, communication, or the many kinds of work that fall outside a clear issue. Models might have seen the repositories and solutions during training, so contamination is a worry, and some tests accept wrong fixes or reject valid ones. High scores on a benchmark can overstate real-world ability. And as models improve, the benchmark itself will saturate, as its predecessors did.
